subtopic: THE SLATER SHOE COMPANY AND ALIEN LABOUR.

speechtext:
Mr. E\ D. MONK (Jacques Cartier). Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to ask the attention of the government to a matter of some importance to the workingmen of the city of Montreal and throughout the country generally. I will read an extract from the minutes of a meeting of the members of the Canadian Federation of the United Shoemakers of Canada, held on the 9th of October instant, at the meeting hall of their society in Montreal :
Extract from the minutes of a meeting of the members of the Canadian Federation of United Shoemakers of Canada, held on the 9th of October instant, at the meeting hall of their society at Montreal.
The following resolution was proposed and unanimously carried :-
That the following facts be brought to the notice of the Dominion government :-

1.	That the Canadian Federation of the United Shoemakers of Canada was founded, several years ago, for the purpose of bringing together Canadian shoemakers, with a view to improving their social conditions and ensuring fairer dealings between employers and employees in the shoemaking industry.
2.	The said association is termed national, being purely Canadian, its membership wholly made up of Canadians, who select their officers in this country and keep their funds in Canada.
3.	The said association has been endorsed by all the boot and shoe manufacturers in the district of Montreal, barring one. The said association has made rapid progress, and comprises at present over 1,700 members ; it has accomplished a great deal in the way of ensuring more equitable dealings between capital and labour, and has given satisfaction to the manufacturers and to employees in the boot and shoe industry.
4.	On the 20th of July last, the Slater Shoe Company, Limited, hoot and shoe manufacturers of Montreal, who employed largely members of the Canadian Federation, without reason or justification decided that its operatives should join the Boot and Shoe Workers Union, an international association, having its leaders and its funds in Boston, United States, and which exacts from its members a weekly contribution of twenty-five. cents, the two-thirds of which are forwarded to the board of management in the United States, while the Canadian Federation requires from its members a contribution of only ten cents per week.
5.	At the same time, the Slater Shoe Company stated that they had decided to adopt the national brand of that foreign association to be stamped on their goods, and had resolved to withdraw from the boot and shoemakers' union of the city of Montreal, who endorsed the Canadian Federation of Shoemakers.
6.	The employees of the company who belong to the Canadian Federation, numbering 500, refused to submit to these tyrannical, unjust and arbitrary terms, and were obliged to leave the employ of the Slater Company on account of this refusal.
7.	The Boot and Shoe Workers' Union aforementioned, whose membership in Montreal is limited to a few hundred, undertook, by all possible means, to supply the said company with hands to replace the members of the Canadian Federation, and tried to recruit men elsewhere.
8.	The Slater Shoe Company, finding itself unable to carry on operations without the help of other operatives to replace those who had left their employ under the circumstances above mentioned, had recourse to the importation of shoemakers from the United States.
9.	The said company despatched emissaries to the United States to recruit hands, and by advertising in various localities in that country and through the efforts and help of the foreign leaders of the international association and their agents, succeeded in bringing to Montreal to work in their factory, about forty or fifty foreign operatives imported from the United States.
10.	Such importation of alien labour is in open violation of the Federal Act 60-61 Victoria, chapter 11, as amended by I Edward VII., chapter 13.
11.	Such infringement of an Act, the object of which is to protect Canadian labour against the competition and importation of alien labour, is extremely hurtful to our workingmen. The aforementioned Act provides that the Dominion government may interfere in cases

subtopic: THE SLATER SHOE COMPANY AND ALIEN LABOUR.
speechtext:
where foreign labour is imported contrary to the provisions of the above statute and may send back to their country of origin hands thus imported, at the expense of those who employ them.
12.	The United States government are strictly enforcing a similar law in their own territory, whenever foreigners are imported to work there. Our government would not only be justifiable, but even should feel themselves in duty bound to act promptly towards the enforcement of the aforementioned statute, with a view to protecting Canadian labour, particularly in the case of a company such as the Slater Shoe Company, who, for several years past, got from the government heavy contracts for the supply of boots and shoes.
13.	The Canadian Federation is prepared to prove all the facts herein stated, if the government are willing to make an investigation into the matter. The Federation wish to protest at the same time against the report which appeared in the 1 Labour Gazette,' to the effect that the strike at the Slater Shoe Company's factory was over.
Therefore, the Canadian Federation requests that the Dominion government should interfere promptly in connection with this difficulty between the Slater Shoe Company and their former employees, members of the Canadian Federation of United Shoemakers of Canada ; that the government, in accordance with the powers conferred by the Act 60-61 Victoria, chapter 11, as amended, should oblige the Slater Shoe Company to send back to the United States the hands imported from that country who are employed in their factory, and that in the event of the company failing to do so, the Dominion government should send these operatives back at the expense of the said Slater Company. The Canadian Federation is ready to reveal the names of the workingmen so imported to persons designated for that purpose by the government to look into the circumstances and make inquiry.
In consequence, the Canadian Federation urgently appeals to the government to enforce the law and to duly protect Canadian labour ; and hopes that the government will do its duty.
That a copy of the present resolution be forwarded to the right honourable Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Prime Minister of Canada, and to Sir William Mulock, the Minister of Labour.
True copy of the minutes of the said meeting.
(Signed) T. BEAUPRE,
President.
(Signed) A. J. DIONNE,
Secretary.
My right hon. friend will see that this is a grave question in a factory which does a considerable quantity of government work. The authorities of the manufactory dismiss a large number of Canadian workingmen, and contrary to law, import from the United States, from Boston and vicinity a certain number of American workmen to replace those Canadian workmen, who, under coercion and contrary to their own interests, are obliged to quit the factory. I will not ask the hon. Minister of Labour (Hon. Sir William Mulock), because I am afraid he has not proved during this session that he has taken up the case of the workingmen with any desire to protect their interests,

but I would like to ask the right hon. First Minister what is being done to put an immediate stop to this state of affairs ?

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. I. TARTE (Montreal, St. Mary's).
subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, although the hon. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) is not in his seat it is my duty to call the attention of the government to a state of affairs that to my knowledge has never existed before. I intend to move the adjournment of the House to put myself in order, seconded by Mr. Bell. The agents of the government newspapers are going to every postmaster in the province of Quebec and insisting on getting from these public officers the names of the subscribers to ail the newspapers which have not either the privilege or the disadvantage of being government organs. I speak from personal knowledge. I speak of facts that I am in a position to establish when I say that they get from nearly every postmaster in the province of Quebec the names of subscribers to newspapers-I say it again-who have not the privilege or the disadvantage of being government organs. I would like to know whether the same privilege would be extended to all the newspapers or if the privilege which has never been exercised to my knowledge during the last twenty-five years Is to be confined to the agents of government newspapers. This is a very serious state of affairs. The postmasters do not any longer keep secret what is going on in their offices. Not only have government officers been allowed to canvass for government papers, but the postmaster of the Public Works Department, a gentleman whom I appointed myself, has been given a leave of absence under the pretext of illness.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: He is not an officer of my department.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: It does not matter, I am addressing myself to this House and the country. I am placing before them a particular state of affairs which is a very serious one. A public officer, the postmaster of the Department of Public Works, has been giveu leave of absence under the pretext of illness and he has been acting as chief circulation agent of the government organ in Montreal. His son, who, I believe, is not of age, has been appointed to his place at $1,200 a year. The gentleman to whom leave of absence on account of illness has been given has not been sick at all. He was not sick and the hon. minister knew he was not sick. I state the fact; he knew he was not sick. He has been canvassing as chief circulation agent of the government organ in Montreal and his son has been receiving 'his salary. In addition to that the postmasters of the province of Quebec have been forced to give the names of the subscribers of newsapers, which, in the estimation of some hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, are not friendly to them, to the agents of government organs. I want to know whether the same privilege will be given to all the newspapers. For instance, will the agents of ' La Patrie ' be allowed to go to the postmasters in the province of Quebec and ask for the names of the subscribers of the newspapers received in their locality ? I will not object at all if the rule is applied to everybody. I do not rise to personally complain. As far as the newspapers I am connected with is concerned vfe have not suffered in spite of what may have been said) in the past. Our circulation is larger to-day than it was a year ago.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext: Yes, that is true today. I observe that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prgfontaine) says hear, hear. I am prepared to issue a challenge to him. I repeat that our circulation is larger to-day. The circulation of our two newspapers is larger to-day than it was a year ago, so that I do not complain personally, only I want to know whether such a state of affairs as that which I have described is to be allowed to continue. Will a postmaster in the province of Ontario be allowed to give* the names of the subscribers of the 'Mail,' or the 'World,' or the * Globe ' and if so I want to know whether the same privilege will be extended to us in the province of Quebec. The hon. Postmaster General. I hope will give us a satisfactory answer on that point.

I do not know that we should go farther on that point. I am only discussing the question of privilege. As to the use that is made of it, it is a very simple thing. This is being done all over the province of Quebec. Provided the same laws apply to all I do not care.
The PRIME MINISTER (Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier)). It is evident that my hon. friend is proceeding under a delusion. He magnifies the work of a probably over-zealous agent into a government system. The hon. gentleman charges that the postmaster of the Public Works Department has obtained leave of absence from the minister under the pretense of illness, and he says the minister knew this official was not ill. I refuse to believe that the minister would give leave of absence, knowing that the official was not ill, but the minister will be here to speak for himself. I believe that if this official asked for leave of absence, he did It in the regular way, and I do not think that the minister had reason to suppose that he was imposed upon, if he was imposed upon.

speechtext: It is a question of fact. If the right hon. gentleman will apply to some of his friends in the House, they will tell him that the minister was approached and asked that Mr. Latour should be sent out as he was a very essentiai agent.

speechtext: We heard a similar statement in this House a few days ago, and I understand the Minister of Public Works did not admit its accuracy. At all events, if the minister has given an improper leave of absence, it will be for the House to deal with the minister who is responsible. It is also stated that this officer is now acting as a canvassing agent for certain newspapers, and that he goes to the postmasters in several parts of the country, and asks to see the lists of subscribers to different newspapers. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has made the charge in such a way as to imply, that the postmasters had received an order from the Post Office Department to allow an agent for papers friendly to the government, to have access to the list of subscribers to other papers. On that point, the hon. gentleman is absolutely under a delusion. No such order has been given by the Postmaster General's department. If any postmasters have done that, they have done it without authority, and on their own responsibility, and without being ordered by i anybody to do it.

speechtext: My point is that I want to know if it is proper for postmasters to act in this way. I can tell my right hon.

speechtext: Perhaps I may be permitted to present my view of it. We are winding- up a session in a debate not of to-day only, but of several days, of misrepresentation. This is in keeping with the tenor of previous debates. The hon. gentleman has sought to convey the impression that the postmasters of this country were more or less, by reason of the authority of or pressure from the government

speechtext: The hon. gentleman said that postmasters were being forced to disclose the names of subscribers of newspapers. I challenge my hon. friend to prove-we will give him a chance to do so if he can-that the government or any officer of the government, with any consent of the government, or with their acquiescence or knowledge, has invited, or pressed, or authorized, or in any way warranted, the postmasters to disclose the names of the addressees of newspapers in any part of Canada. If my hon. friend had been attending to his duties in parliament he would not have felt it necessary to raise this question to-day; because in Committee of Supply the other day it was, raised by an hon. gentleman opposite, and I was asked to state my attitude in regard to the matter. The view I announced then is my view to-day, and it has been the attitude of the government ever since this government has been in existence. I stated then, and I state now, the information which postmasters possess as to the names of the addressees of mail matter of any kind, whether it consists of letters, parcels, newspapers or any other matter that may pass through the mails, is confidential; and they are not warranted in disclosing that information to any human being except the addressees themselves. I stated that in the most unqualified way. I stated then, and I state now, that if any hon. gentleman will specify the name of any officer of my department who has been guilty of any breach of confidence, I will feel it my duty to discipline that officer in a way appropriate to his offence. Is that a fair attitude ? Does my hon. friend take exception to it ?

speechtext: I do not take exception to that statement; very far from it. My hon. friend has made the right statement, and I congratulate him upon it. It is worthy of a Minister of the Crown. But I state again that over one hundred postmasters in the province of Quebec and in other provinces also have given freely the information which I have stated to the House. If my hon. friend wants me to make charges against them all in order that he may dismiss them, I am prepared to do it, although I do not wish any ill-luck to anybody; but these are the facts of the case. I will give him, with pleasure, the names of these officers, if he wishes to have them. What I meant to convey was this, that the postmasters, being approached by agents of the party in power, thought they were obliged to give that information, and they have given it freely. I am glad my hon. friend the Postmaster General has vindicated his position, and I congratulate him on the statement which he has just made and which I accept altogether.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext:
Then 1 my hon. friend will see that it is only fair

for him to modify his views. He overstated wliat he had in his mind.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: I have not.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit me to suggest that perhaps now he owes a duty to this House. He as a man of affairs knows that men enjoying- the good will of a particular party, the party in power for the moment, may go about canvassing. Our supporters, our friends, our sympathizers are legion in number, and they perhaps act as agents to procure subscribers for newspapers. Men who are engaged in canvassing for anything are zealous, and these men may go to a postmaster, and may bring to bear whatever arguments may occur to them in order to obtain such assistance as will enable them to succeed in their enterprises; but that does not mean that they are agents for the government or have any authority from the government. There is no human being /authorized by the government to exact such information as my hon. friend says has been imparted by postmasters. The postmasters themselves ought to be possessed of sufficient intelligence to know that any person who drops in and asks them for the names of the addressees of mail matter, have not any authority to demand it, simply because they choose to ask for it; and I would ask my hon. friend, since he says he can do so, to furnish me with the names of the postmasters who he says have been transgressors; and, as 1 stated before, these cases will be duly investigated, and the postmasters will be disciplined. The officers will of course be given an opportunity to explain what they have done, and steps will be taken to prevent any repetition of such action in the future.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: Would it not be well for the hon. gentleman to issue instructions to the postmasters generally that they must keep confidential what my hon. friend wants to be kept confidential ? I accept with pleasure the hon. gentleman's offer, and I undertake to give him the names of dozens and dozens of postmasters

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: Hundreds.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: Dozens and dozens of names from hundreds of postmasters. I will undertake, with pleasure, to give the names to my hon. friend; and if he feels that the proper discipline would be dismissal, it is for him to say.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext:
Well, I will undertake that the postmasters who he says have transgressed will never repeat the offence. Throughout the whole of this country there has been a practice for many years of postmasters acting as agents for newspapers, and they are not interfered with. Postmasters are permitted to act as agents to receive subscriptions for all papers, without regard to the politics of the Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
papers. If the House desires that that practice should be put an end to, the government and the department will give every consideration to that view. It will cut both ways.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: I understood that there was a charge made in this House, not only to-day, but some two weeks ago, that an officer of the government, while ostensibly absent on his vacation, had been engaged in canvassing for a newspaper, and had been obtaining from postmasters in the province of Quebec the names of subscribers to certain newspapers in that province.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: I do not make the charge directly against that officer. I make the general charge that postmasters in the province of Quebec have given information to agents of government organs. I do not know whether Mr. Latour himself has gone to these postmasters.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: I do not know how that may be. The matter was discussed in the House some ten days ago, and I think it would have been very well for the Postmaster General then to have issued the circular which he now proposes to issue. The men who are engaged in this work are inducing the postmasters to commit a breach of the law. Is it not an offence under the Post Office Act, or a breach of the regulations of the department, for postmasters to communicate information of this kind ? Would mv hon. friend inform me as to that ?

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: I cannot say what the regulations are ; but if there is no regulation covering the case, there ought to be one. I think I have made my view quite clear. Regulation or no regulation, the duty rests upon the postmaster to observe the strictest confidence as to the names of addressees. I would not think a regulation was necessary in order to impress that duty on a postmaster. And the other evening when the matter was brought up, no specific charge was made ; the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Pope) made a state-men that this particular officer had been engaged in the work, and that night I asked the member for Compton to give me the information which I now ask from Jhe hon. member for St. Mary's division, Montreal (Mr. Tarte), to give me the names of the officers whom he says have offended. I promised to investigate the charge if that information was given me, but it has not yet been given, and again we have an indefinite charge made.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: I will give the information.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext:
I was in hopes that my hon. friend the Postmaster General could have told us what the law in regard to this is. I agree with him that if there is no regulation there should be one, and if

there is a regulation then we have a provision in the statutes that any man who violates that regulation is guilty of a misdemeanour. The men who are going through the province of Quebec doing this work, are engaged in the work of inducing officers of the Crown to commit a violation of the law. It would be the duty of the government, upon the matter having been brought to their attention, to take legal proceedings against these men who are corrupting officers of the law, if the provisions of the law are sufficient for the purpose, and if the law is not sufficient I hope it will be amended so that this work will be stopped. The Postmaster General challenges us to show that lxis department or any officer of his department has been guilty of this conduct.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: I understood that the Postmaster General made this challenge to the hon. member for St. Mary's division, Montreal (Hon. Mr. Tarte) ; I understood my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) to say that the Postmaster General challenged the opposition.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext:
I presume that there is some point in my friend's observation, but I do not exactly see it at present. Whether the officers of the department are doing this or not-and I am bound to take the statement of the Postmaster General that they are not doing it-certain persons representing organs of the government, are going, with the pretended authority of this government, to postmasters in Quebec and by means of that false claim, however false it may be, are obtaining information to which they are not entitled. That is one point of the observations of the hon. member for St. Mary's division, Montreal (Hon. Mr. Tarte), and it is a matter which invites the attention of the government, because whether or not any officer of the department is guilty of these acts, they cannot shut their eyes to the fact that their own supporters are, by their false pretenses and claims, coercing the postmasters of Quebec. They urge the fact that they are supporting the party in power, and they claim to have the right to have these postmasters dismissed or otherwise dealt with in case they do not furnish that information. I say that this demands the immediate attention of the government, and that the government should take proceedings against the postmasters themselves, but more especially against the men who are urging the postmasters, by threats of poltical influence, to do that which it is improper to do, and which, as I understand the law, it is unlawful to do. My hon. friend may issue as many challenges as he likes about the officers of the department, but my understanding is that this is being done by supporters of the government under the claim that they have the force and power of the government behind them. An admittedly
wrong thing is being done, even according to the statements of the Postmaster General, who says that he does not know whether there is such a regulation. But he admits that if there is not a regulation there ought to be one. Under these circumstances I think that some action should have been taken by the Postmaster General before this; action cannot be taken by him too promptly under the circumstances that have been disclosed to the House to-day. And let me tell my hon. friend the Postmaster General who spoke in a somewhat sneering way of the absence from the House of my hon. friend from St. Mary's division (Hon. Mr. Tarte), that I do not think any member of the government is in a position to say very much about that, because we have now before us this matter involving the Department of Public Works, and the Minister of Public Works cannot be found to answer the statement of the hon. member for St. Mary's division, Montreal. We have had ministers of the Crown very frequently absent from' their places in this House when we were discussing estimates in regard to which they could have given information that was desired. I quite understand that this absence is sometimes necessary, but yet I might advert to the fact that the Solicitor General-I do not know for what reason- has hardly made an appearance in the House during the present session. If we come to investigate the absence of presence of members, the hon. member for St. Mary's division can at least say that he has been in his seat in the House during this session about as much as any minister of the Crown.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: I believe I have, yes.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: I do hope that the Postmaster General will give this matter the attention which its importance demands, and I am led to believe that he will give it that attention by the fact that he has to-day very properly and promptly said that if the names of these postmasters are furnished to him he will take steps to investigate. But I do not think he should stop there ; he should take steps to punish the men who have been inciting postmasters in Quebec and in Ontario as well-if the statement of the hon. member for St. Mary's division can be substantiated-under the guise of the pretended authority of this government, to commit a breach of their duty and of the law.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that I should immediately take steps to deal with this subject. Permit me to suggest that perhaps a duty is cast on those who say that they possess information as to the misconduct complained of. Some days ago it was stated by the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Pope) that certain postmasters had disclosed confidential information and had given the names of subscribers to newspapers. I then asked the hon. gen-

tleinan to furnish me with the names of the postmasters whom he said had transgressed, and that information was promised to me. Some days have elapsed, but that information has not yet been given to me. How could I investigate the cases when 1 did not know the names of the accused ? I then pointed out that we have ten thousand and more postmasters.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: I was not urging action with respect to names not furnished ; I admit at once that it would be impossible to do that, but I say that the names have been promised to-day, and when these names are furnished he should proceed to punish not only the postmasters, but those who urged them to commit a breach of the law.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: I told the House that when the names, are furnished to me I will then, for the first time, be in a position to intelligently investigate this charge. Cau my hon. friend give me the names of the officer of my department whom he stated in the House yesterday had made certain threats against an express company ?

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: I do not know the name of the officer ; I promised to give it yesterday, but the matter escaped my mind. I will give it to my hon. friend today. The name of the officer can be procured, I think, because the information has been furnished to me by the express company which was threatened.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: The question raised by the Postmaster General as to whether it is proper for postmasters to act as agents for the newspapers is a very important question. I know, as a matter of fact, that in the constituency which I have the honour to represent there have been in the past, and there may be now, postmasters who are acting as agents for a very large and important newspaper in the city of Montreal. I consider such acts very reprehensible, as against public interests and against the other newspapers, for the simple reason that such postmasters know what is the circulation of every newspaper that goes through their office. It is very unfair to the general public that any postmaster should be permitted to act as the agent of any newspaper. I wish to emphasize the point raised by the Postmaster General, and trust he will take action to prevent any postmaster acting in any such capacity.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: I must disagree with my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson). The salary of many postmasters throughout the country is very small, and I see no harm in a postmaster earning an honest dollar by acting as agent for a newspaper.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext:
This practice, to which our attention has been Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
drawn by the hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte), is not confined at all to the province of Quebec. To my knowledge these agents of newspapers supporting the government are travelling through the country seeking to obtain from the postmasters information as to the subscribers to all newspapers not friendly to the government. The postmasters are not the real culprits. We can find the remedy right here. One remedy would be for the Postmaster General to advise the postmasters not to give this information. They may not view the matter seriously and may give information to one side or the other without thinking they are doing great harm, and they may readily yield to the pressure brought on them by the agents of newspapers supporting the government. Another remedy would be for members of the government, who are behind these newspapers, to call off these men who are seeking this information. The real evil is not so much the postmasters giving the information as the agents of the government demanding it from them.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: They are not agents of the government.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: They are in an indirect sense.	'

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: In no sense.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman and his friends profit by it. My hon. friend beside me suggests that each minister has a paper of his own. We have no objection to agents of government newspapers going around the country getting information, but we object to its being furnished by the postmasters. The Postmaster General need not wait for an inquiry. All he need do is inform the postmasters what is their duty.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: I see an announcement in the 'Citizen' this morning which I would draw to the attention of the hon. the Postmaster General. It is to the effect that two special trains will leave the capital to-day with Conservative campaign literature.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext: The hon-. gentleman is out of order. That has no connection with the question before the Chair.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER AGENTS AND POSTMASTERS IN QUEBEC.
speechtext:
To my mind the difficulty brought up by the hon. member for Montreal (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has its origin in the defective regulations of the department. The regulation plainly conveys to any postmaster the idea that he is free to give every information respecting the subscribers to newspapers which go through his office. Here is the regulation :
Article 176. No information can be given respecting letters which pass through the post office except to the persons to whom they are addressed and the senders on inquiry respecting delivery. The post-masters are n-ot permitted to

furnish any information respecting the names and addresses of persons who. receive correspondence at their respective offices.
There is nothing in that regulation regarding newspapers. It is entirely restricted to letters. An agent therefore could readily persuade the postmaster that the intention of the government was that he should give that information. I think that until these regulations are revised and reprinted in the postal guide, a special regulation should at once be sent out to all the postmasters, making this rule 170 applicable to newspapers as well as to letters.
Motion to adjourn (Hon. Mr. Tarte) negatived.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Before the Orders of the Day are called, I want to ask if the hon. First Minister and the hon. Postmaster General have had a conference and what explanation he has to give the House ?

I am pleased to inform my hon. friend that the difficulty to which he alludes has been successfully overcome. It involved considerable effort and a considerable expenditure of money, but we have done all that the resources of the country will permit. We ordered an additional supply of 1,000 mail hags, but I am sorry to say that that number was inadequate, and we have had to order 2,000. The delivery of these bags commences this afternoon and will continue rapidly, so that we hope soon to be able to place at the disposal of hon. gentlemen opposite all the bags now used in this very interesting and important public work. With reference to the dissemination of this literature, which my hon. friend characterized rather irreverently as ' stuff '-
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock).

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The right kind of stuff, too.

A rose by any other name would smell as sweet.
1 say with reference to this literature that we have made arrangements which I trust will successfully solve the difficulty. It is quite true that we have already chartered one special train, which will leave Ottawa as soon as the staff of special employees can be obtained' to man it, I think, by tonight. You will observe a mountain of literature already adorning the front of the House of Commons, and that trainload is being conveyed to the station as rapidly as the available supply in this city will admit, and as fast as steam will carry It to its destination it will be despatched. I am sorry to say-no, I am not sorry, but the fact is that a second train, and perhaps a third train will be necessary. But our duty, we think, is first of all to clear the lobbies and
halls of this building, as soon as that interesting task is performed, we will then proceed to try and clear out all the floor space that is occupied by this literature in the city post office. I hope that in the course of at least three days we will have despatched all these pieces to their destination, and they will afford, I am sure, most interesting reading to the addressees, and perhaps they will then consider, upon a careful perusal of them, whether the game has been worth the candle, whether the cost to which the country lias been put is fully warranted by this very extraordinary procedure. However, it is probable that the country will demand some amendment of the franking privilege. It certainly has been grossly abused.	,
By none more so than by the hon. gentlemen opposite.
There is no case on record since Canada had an existence where such an abuse of the system has occurred as in the present instance.

It is a somewhat remarkable thing that a certain amount of mail matter which, as we were told yesterday, could not. be forwarded to its destination inside of six weeks, is now to be forwarded in 24 hours.
I made no such statement.

That shows what my hon. friend the Postmaster General is capable of, under a little pressure ; and I would suggest to my right hon. friend that if he is ever met with difficulties of this kind put forward by the Postmaster General, ail he has to do is to exercise a little pressure upon him such as was exercised by my hon. friend the member from Leeds and Grenville (Mr. Taylor) yesterday, and he will find him capable of almost any feat. Why, yesterday this mail matter paralyzed the Ottawa office, it was piled up in mountains. it would require six weeks of special exertion to forward it to its destination. But only last night an officer of the hon. gentleman's department said it could all be cleared out within 24 hours. My hon. friend himself has practically repeated the same thing to-day, and he desires to make a little political capital by talking of the expenditure of public money. But he has never contradicted the statement that the equivalent of 25 or 30 bags have been sent out daily by hon. gentlemen opposite during the past six. or seven, or -eight weeks. He has never contradicted that statement, nor has any hon. gentleman on the other side contradicted the statement that practically during all these weeks the addressing of envelopes has been done by servants of this country, paid by the people of this country, for hon. gentlemen opposite. That charge was made

some days ago in the House, and I have not heard up to this time any absolute denial of it, except that I believe it was denied by the gentleman in charge of the Department of Public Works. The Postmaster General thinks, under these circumstances, that he is making a little political capital by talking of the expenditure of public money in forwarding this literature, which I venture to say, does not amount to in bulk or in cost of transmission to one-half of the campaign literature which has been forwarded by hon. gentlemen themselves during the present session. I am here reminded of the fact that my right hon. friend the Min-iter of Trade and Commerce, if we are to talk about the franking privileges, distributed I do not know how many hundred thousand copies of a speech of his_ some years ago, when the House was not in session, and in violation of the rules which were laid down by Order in Council with respect to transmission of documents of that kind out of session ; and I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce was invited at that time to contribute the sum of $25,000 to the treasury of Canada, being the amount which he ought to have paid for the distribution of that literature. I do not know whether that is the exact amount. The Minister of Trade and Commerce will, no doubt, make it good in time, because I am sure he expects to pay it before he ends his public career. It may not be convenient for him to do it at present, but we all appreciate the fact that he intends to do it at some time or other, and I do not think the department will be disposed to charge him interest on it. However, I am very glad indeed that the Postmaster General has been able to cope with this difficulty, and that we shall have these mail bags removed that have so long remained here, owing, so far as we can judge, to the fact that his department was not disposed to make a reasonable and moderate effort to forward this matter to its destination.

The hon. the leader of the opposition is developing, if he will permit me to say so, a disposition to present a case in a very unfair light. I explained to him, I think, and it was something he well knows, that there is a vast difference between the surplus space that is afforded in mail cars for the extra literature such as this, and the case of a whole train, or a special train, set apart exclusively for work of that kind. The regular trains of the country have to carry much mail matter for the general public. What I stated was that the service supposed to be available for the extra postal matter here would not admit of more than 40 bags per day being handled in these postal cars. But, under the special arrangements which have been made, we have engaged trains and set them apart exclusively for this service, and with these extra trains we expect to be Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
able to solve this problem within the next three days.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, I would ask to be allowed to put myself right in reference to a matter with which I was occupied in my capacity of Minister of Public Works. I have read some reflections in the press regarding the matter. I refer to the use by Mr. Lacoste of one of the boats of the Department of Public Works named the ' Eureka.' speechtext: The only information which we have on that point is what is common property, and has been published in the newspapers. On the Order being called for the House to go into committee on certain resolutions respecting the granting of aid to the Quebec bridge :

In moving that you do now leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, for the purpose, of having the House consider in committee certain resolutions which have been submitted with respect to the granting of aid to the Quebec bridge, I wish to take advantage of the opportunity to make a brief statement. The Importance of , another bridge across the St. Lawrence, at or near the city of Quebec, has been recognized for many years by gentlemen on both sides of the House. Several years ago this government came to the conclusion that the time for action had arrived, anl it was authorized to assist the company which had undertaken to bring about the construction of that bridge. A company was formed in the city of Quebec, with a capital of $200,000, with power to issue bonds in the usual way in connection with such public undertakings. The movement was recognized as one of



great importance in the city of Quebec, in the province of Quebec and in the Dominion generally. The city of Quebec manifested its substantial interest in the movement by contributing a subsidy' to the bridge of $300,000 ; the government of the province of Quebec manifested its interest in the enterprise bv contributing a subsidy of $250,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: Is that an absolute gift ?

Yes, in both cases a free and absolute gift, and the money has been paid. The government of the Dominion also agreed to aid the undertaking by a guarantee of $1,000,000. The grants given by the city of Quebec, and by the government of Quebec have been paid, and of the grant offered by the parliament of Canada of $1,000,000, there has been paid the sum of $374,353. The company, with a capital of $200,000 nominally, have actually paid up and put into the treasury $65,585 of their private funds. With the capital of the company, with the aids granted by the city of Quebec, the province of Quebec and the Dominion of Canada, and with the power to issue bonds, the company proceeded to construct the bridge and they have made very considerable progress.
What has actually been paid by the government here ?

Three hundred and seventy-four thousand three hundred and fifty-three dollars. The company proceeded to let contracts and enter upon the undertaking. The substructure has been completed, and a portion of the superstructure. The work actually done by the company up to the present time represents an expenditure of $1,416,394. That expenditure has been made from private capital, from the gift of the province of Quebec, which has been paid in full, from the gift of the city of Quebec, which has also been paid in full, and from the gift of the Dominion government, which was $1,000,000, but which has been paid to the extent of only $374,353. The company have been obliged to issue bonds to assist the undertaking, and these bonds to the amount of $472,000 are outstanding. These bonds were given to the contractor in part payment, and he accepted them at 60 per cent of their face value ; so that while they represent a bonded indebtedness upon the enterprise of $472,000, the actual cash received from them was $283,279. There is now due to the contractors and others $779,551. This includes, however, the $472,000 of bonds at tlieir par value.
To whom is the balance of $779,000 due ?
There is a ,\ush balance due the contractors, besides

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
the outstanding issue of bonds. There are some charges for engineering and other things, but it is substantially due to the contractors. The company find themselves unable to prosecute the undertaking further, although the commercial prospect of the bridge is fairly good. I think most people who have looked into it as a business enterprise will agree to that. But even when an enterprise has an excellent prospect of commercial success, it is not easy to raise capital for a very large undertaking. This is a very large undertaking. The total cost of the bridge is estimated by Mr. Colling-wood Schreiber, the chief engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals, at $7,503,725. That includes not merely the bridge 'proper, but the approaches, and the terminal facilities in the city of Quebec.
Now, inasmuch as the company are not likely to be able to prosecute the work successfully, the government have deemed it wise to come to the relief of the company and the enterprise, and to change their form of aid. As I have already stated, we have granted $1,000,000, of which only $374,353 has been paid. The remainder is still in the treasury of Canada. We propose to cancel that balance, and to say that the company shall receive no further aid in the way of a subsidy or a gift, but that instead we shall grant them aid in the form of a guarantee, which we think, from the information which we have, will not ultimately cost the Dominion one cent. We quite realize that in all guarantees there is a measure of risk ; but so far as information is obtainable Horn competent railway men, we think there is a fair ground for the statement that the earnings of this enterprise will meet all its obligations, and that in adopting the form of a guarantee instead of actually contributing anything more to the bridge, we are cancelling an obligation of some $600,000 or more, which we would otherwise be obliged to pay. Of course, we give the company more valuable assistance for the moment by the guarantee, because by that means the enterprise will be carried to a success. With our grant of $l,000,o00, the company would not have been able to finance the enterprise so successfully as they will be with the guarantee. We propose, therefore, to guarantee a sum of money, in the form of bonds bearing 3 per cent interest and running fifty years, to a sufficient extent to meet the outstanding indebtedness and to complete the bridge.
But when we come to deal with the question of outstanding indebtedness, we find, as I have pointed out, that while as respects the bonds there is an indebtedness of $472,000, the actual value of the work which they represent is only $283,279, the difference representing a discount on the bonds, which the contractors were only willing to take on the basis of 60 cents on the dollar. We think we ought not to be called on to cover that discount or deficiency by a gov-

eminent guarantee. It is perhaps very common, in connection with the financing of an undertaking of this character, that bonds have to be sold at a discount. The discount in this case is perhaps larger than usual. However, the fact remains that there is outstanding in bonds secured by first mortgage on this bridge, the sum of $472,000, while the actual value represented in cash we have placed at $283,279. We think the difference, representing a discount of $188,000, should be met by the company themselves, and should not be covered by the government guarantee. We have, therefore, required them to subscribe for and pay up new capital to the amount of $200,000, which will practically all be applied to the payment of so much of these bonds as represent the discount. So that in applying our guarantee to the debts of the company, we shall be applying it only to that portion for which we have value received, while that portion which does not represent value received, but which represents a discount on the bonds, must be provided for by a further subscription and payment of private capital.
The company, as it stands now, has an actual paid-up capital stock of some $65,000, and it will issue a further sum of $200,000, making a total capital subscribed and paid up of $205,000 ; and we provide that no new stock of any kind shall be issued upon the undertaking, except the bonds which are to be guaranteed by the government, and that no liabilities can be incurred in the meantime except with the consent of the government ; so that the security which the government will have, will be, we think, very good.
The amount required to pay the outstanding debts and to complete the undertaking is estimated at $6,866,882. But that includes the payment of these bonds at par. We, therefore, deduct from that amount $188,721, which the private capitalists are obliged to provide for. That brings the balance required to pay the debts and complete the undertaking to $6,678,200. That amount we propose to guarantee in bonds bearing interest at 3 per cent for fifty years. We propose that the interest of the government shall be protected by having three directors on the board.
Do you repay the bonds themselves, or only guarantee the interest ?

Wo guarantee both the principal and interest. On the question of the earning powers of the bridge, we have some information which has already been laid before the House in the document entitled : ' Papers relating to the Quebec Bridge.' We have had estimates as to the probable number of cars which will use the bridge, and as to the probable revenue from various sources. There are a number of railways which will 460J
use the bridge immediately, because they touch both sides of the river; and undoubtedly, with the early development of trade, especially in connection with the new transcontinental railway, which will cross the Quebec bridge, there is no reason to doubt that any returns based on the present traffic will be sound and safe, because there is every prospect of a large increase at no distant date. We have information as to the probable earnings of the bridge from various sources. The late Mr. Walter Shanly, an eminent engineer, made an estimate as far back as 1885, in which he placed the earnings at $250,400. Mr. Walsh, the general passenger agent of the Quebec Central, in 1897 estimated the earnings at $259,164. Mr. .1. G. Scott, the general manager of the Bake St. John Railway, in 1899, confirmed the estimate of Mr. Shanly, placing the figures at $250,000. And Mr. Grundy, of the Quebec Central, a gentleman of high standing, who still takes a very deep interest in this work, has estimated the earnings at substantially the same amount as Mr. Shanly and Mr. Walsh. Substantially therefore these gentlemen, the late Mr. Shanly, Mr. Walsh, of the Quebec Central, Mr. Scott, of the Quebec and Lake St. John, and Mr. Grundy, estimated some years ago that the earnings would be $250,000 per year.
And we did not know anything then about the transcontinental.

No; my hon. friend, with his natural sense of fairness, points out that at that time they knew nothing about the transcontinental project. Nor did they even know that the Great Northern was to be constructed. The conditions have therefore been changed since these reports were made, but whatever change has taken place is in favour of the enterprise, because the volume of business is increasing. We have had inquiries made very recently by officers of our own government, officers of the Intercolonial, into the probable earnings of the bridge. Mr. Tiffin, the general traffic manager of the Intercolonial, has made a report on the subject, the substance of which will be found in a letter addressed to me by Mr. Schreiber, chief engineer of government railways, dated Ottawa, September the 19th. Mr. Schreiber sums up as follows :
With reference to the matter of the probable extent of traffic over the Quebec bridge, when constructed, as to which you desire some Information. I have to state that, under date the 1st instant, Mr. Tiffin, the traffic manager of the Intercolonial Railway, has furnished an estimate of the number of cars that, it may be anticipated!, would cross the ' Quebec bridge ' dally, not taking into consideration traffic that may arise from the construction of the proposed Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. This estimate is as follows :



Estimated number of cars daily.
Intercolonial' Railway	 130
Grand Trunk Railway	 75
Quebec Central Railway	 71
Total	 276
Extended to a full year, the aggregate is^ 276 cars per day plus 313 days equal 86,388 cars, which at $4 each, amounts to $345,552 per annum.
As to the rate of $4 per car, I find that It is higher than the rates paid in Canada at some points, but lower than the rates paid on some of the large bridges in the United States.
Did you take the working expenses into account ?

I have not come to that. I am speaking of the possible earning powers. We have therefore, on the advice of the chief engineer of railways and canals, the probable earnings estimated at $345,552 per annum. Let us see now what our obligations are on the other side. Three per cent on the amount to be guaranteed will be $200,346. We are providing in addition that there shall be one-half per cent on the amount of guaranteed bonds set apart each year for the purpose of a sinking fund. That will not be sufficient to extinguish the loan in the fifty years. It will take about sixty-five years to extinguish the whole loan at that rate, but, in the common practice, we do not aim at extinguishing the whole loan but at having a very substantial sinking fund to assist in doing so. If this enterprise should continue in the hands of the company to the end of the fifty years, we shall have a sinking fund sufficient to extinguish about $3,750,000 of the debt, and there will be no difficulty whatever in financing the balance upon a new issue of bonds. However, I do not anticipate that that contingency will ever arise. No doubt long before that this bridge will be taken over and become the property of the government. We shall have annual) interest, $200,346; the half per cent sinking fund, $33,391; or a total of $233,737 to pay every year. The working expenses are estimated by Mr. Frank Grundy of the Quebec Central at $85,000. Adding this to the $233,737 gives a total of $318,737, against which we shall hare an income, which is estimated according to the estimates I have already given, confirmed by the chief engineer of railways and canals, at $345,552.
Do the working expenses include repairs and depreciation ?

Under our contract repairs and renewals are considered as working expenses, and 1 take it for granted that these working expenses are included in the estimates I have given I am not sure whether Mr. Grundy did include working expenses, but I assume he did because he is a very capable railway man and would no doubt include them in his calculation.
I thought 1 understood the hon. gentleman to say that the interest would be about $200,000. But three per cent on $8,000,000 makes $240,000.

The amount we are guaranteeing is not $8,000,000 but $6,678,200. The whole cost is estimated at $7,500,000, but the amount we shall require to pay off existing indebtedness, not including discount on the bonds, and to complete the undertaking we estimate at $6,678,200. We have therefore a very safe margin on which to base our assurance that this bridge will, from the beginning, guarantee us against any loss; and while, by the step we are taking, we shall be giving aid in a better form and securing the completion of the bridge, we shall on the other hand not be adding to the obligations of the country ultimately, and be avoiding the payment of over $600,000, whicli otherwise we would be obliged to pay out of the million dollar grant already authorized and only partially paid.
My hon. friend (Mr. Fitzpatrick) reminds me too that in this estimate of the cost we are including the customs duty to an amount approximating from $700,000 to $800,000, which will come back directly into the treasury. That is an additional fact to be taken into account.
While for the present we are assuming that it will be wise to allow this enterprise to remain in the hands of the company and let them complete the undertaking, we do not look forward to its remaining permanently in the company's hands. In view of the importance of the bridge and the number of railways which will pass over it and its relations to the new road we are about to construct, and for various other reasons, wre think it is highly probable that, at no distant date, the government of Canada, no matter who may be in power, will desire to take possession of the road as a national work. Therefore, we are providing in the contract that we shall have power to take possession of the enterprise any time after completion, upon one month's notice. If we do, we shall then pay to the company the amount of net cash they put into the enterprise, which, according to the contract, will be $265,000, with interest at the rate of five per cent, less any dividend that may have been earned in the meantime. And we will pay them a premium of ten per cent on the par value of their stock, which is not an unusual thing in taking over an enterprise. That par value as fixed in the contract will be $265,000. Thus they will receive their money back with interest at five per cent, less any dividends which may be earned, and ten per cent advance on the money they have put iu.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: How soon does the hon. minister expect that the government will be obliged to take over the undertaking ?
The government will not be obliged to take it over at all.

But, as a matter of policy, my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Fielding) said that undoubtedly before long the undertaking will be taken over and become the property of the government. My hon. friend has touched on that point, and I would like to ask him if it is a matter of two or three years, or if it is to be taken over simultaneously with the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific ?

That would be a matter for consideration. The company is allowed three years in which to complete the undertaking, and from the moment that the undertaking is completed we will have the right to take it over upon one mouth's notice. We can take it over at any time after 1906, whether the road is completed or not. On whichever event shall first happen, either the completion of the road or the arrival of that date three years hence, the government shall have the right to take over the undertaking, and I am inclined to think, as I said before, that any government which is in power will find at no distant date that it will be to the advantage of the Dominion to take over that bridge. However, there has been no arrangement in that form, but we have thought it wise to protect the people's right to acquire that bridge at any time after its completion or after 1906.
Is any time fixed in the contract at which that bridge is to be completed ?

It is to be completed on the 1st December, 1906. In addition to that, the Minister of Justice calls my attention to the fact that if, during construction, we are not satisfied with the progress made, if the road is not being pushed forward to successful completion, the government shall have the right to take it over, apart from the general right they would possess afterwards. If we should take over the bridge at any time we would find ourselves in this position : The Quebec government would 'have contributed $250,000, the city of Quebec would have contributed $300,000; the government of Canada would have contributed in cash $374,000. So long as the enterprise remains in the hands of the company we treat these sums as free gifts, as they were intended to be, to the enterprise ; but if the Dominion takes over the bridge, we shall then become accountable to the government of the province of Quebec and to the city of Quebec to the extent of the money they have placed in the bridge.
Why should you pay them for their advances ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Because we think that if we take possession of the property as a national work, we should then be willing to account for these advances, but we become accountable to the province and the city of Quebec only for profits which the bridge may earn. We shall, under the contract which we have made- with the company, have the right to take possession of the bridge, and the bridge becomes the property of the Dominion of Canada without any question as to title whatever. We do not recognize any title of the government of Quebec or of the city of Quebec in the bridge, but we do recognize the fact that they have contributed their respective sums of $250,000 and $300.000, and we will place these contributions in precisely the same position as the $374,000 which we have contributed. If the bridge earns anything beyond its working expenses and beyond the interest on its bonded indebtedness, if there are profits, we will divide these profits equitably among the contributors of the three amounts, but there shall not be paid to the government of Quebec or to the city of Quebec more than three per cent interest on the amount of their contributions. If the bridge does not earn anything beyond the working expenses and the interest on the bonded indebtedness, neither the city of Quebec nor the province of Quebec will receive a cent
Have you fully provided for that ?

It is in -the contract, section 21. If it becomes a profitable enterprise and we are making money out of it, we will account to the province of Quebec and the city of Quebec for three per cent on their money so long as we are making money out of it. If we do not earn money, neither the city nor the province of Quebec can receive a penny. They *will have no title, but will have what I may call a deferred interest in the bridge to the extent of the amount they have contributed, and we may at any time extinguish that by paying the amount they have contributed to the bridge.
Have they any lien on the bridge ?
None whatever.
Why, then, do you create one ?

We do not so long as the bridge remains in the hands of the company. They will give that as a free gift, but if we dispossess the company, take the bridge over and make money out of it, we think we should account to the city and province of Quebec for their share or pay off the indebtedness.

Did I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the division of profits
14C99

was to be made on the sum contributed by the government, the $374,000, as against the contributions of the city and province of Quebec, or as against the whole sum which the government will advance in taking over the bridge ?

The $374,000 will be the only sum ; if we take the bridge over we will have the bonded indebtedness to carry, and that will be the first charge before any one can get any money other than the working expenses.

Would it not be more advisable, in view of the government intending to take over this bridge, to simply guarantee the $472,000 bonds instead of contracting this issue of $200,000 of stock, which they may have to take over at a premium ? Would it not be better to simply guarantee the $472,000 at once and be done with it ?
The MINISTER OB' FINANCE. No ; because in this case we will oblige the company to pay the $188,000 themselves out of their own pocket. No new stock can be created under this contract. The amount we will have to pay as premium on the stock will be one-tenth of the $265,000, or $26,500. That is the limit of the premium, and it is a small amount.
Do you think that you can get the stockholders to put their hands into their pockets and pay the $200,000 ?
They must pay the $200,000 more of their own money, every dollar of which must be paid up before they get this guarantee.
That is a good investment; they get 5 per cent interest and 10 per cent premium.
It is a good investment, except that it might be fifty years before they can get it.
That is very doubtful.
I say frankly that I think some of these days the bridge will be taken over. Of course, we cannot guarantee that a good government like the present will be here forever.
Would it not be more advisable for the government to take it over at once as their own property and complete it ?

There is something to be said in favour of that suggestion, but after full investigation we have concluded, since the company have made negotiations and have carried on some of the work, that we had better let them finish the work.
Does the hon. minister consider the clause in this contract sufficient to guard the expenditure of this money ;
that is, that the money shall be expended only in the construction of this bridge ? Are there sufficient guards thrown around the expenditure of the proceeds of these (bonds ?

We think we have sufficiently protected it in that respect. Money can only be paid for value put into the bridge upon the certificate of the government engineer.
At one o'clock, committee took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is a great pity that a matter of this importance has been brought to the attention of the House on the last day of the session ; I mean that to-day we are called upon to discuss a scheme of great magnitude, a very interesting scheme, and we have really not the time to bring to the consideration of that project its importance deserves. I see no necessity for such a wonderful and hasty proceeding. The condition of the Quebec bridge, its need of assistance, existed prior to the meeting of this House on the 12th of March last. It was fully discussed during the sitting of the Quebec legislature ; it formed the subject of a very careful investigation there, and of a lengthy discussion ; and it was stated during that discussion, as my hon. friend the Minister of Justice knows, by the Prime Minister of Quebec himself, the president of this undertaking, that he would apply to the Dominion government for assistance. He was asked in the legislature if he contemplated seeking assistance from the city of Quebec and he said that he did not, neither did he contemplate seeking assistance from the legislature ; and if I am correctly informed, when asked whether he intended to apply for it here in Ottawa before the meeting of this legislature, he stated that he did. Under these circumstances, does it not appear rather unfair to the House that my hon. friend the Minister of Justice should, in the last hours, in the last minutes, one might almost say, of this session, come dow-n with such a complicated plan as the one which he 'has presented to this House ? I mention this because I have always been favourable to that project, and the Conservative party, as members of this House are well aware, was committed to assisting the construction of the Quebec bridge before 1896. Circumstances of which I have little knowledge prevented the party then in power from carrying out its pledge. But the project was sanctioned, the necessity of that undertaking was admitted, and it was merely a question of knowing how best to help carry out that great enterprise. Therefore there is no difference of opinion in regard to the policy, at least that is the way I understand it; the only difference of opinon is as to the way in which the 1 thing can best be done.

Now, what I submit to this House, briefly, is that under the agreement of my hon. friend which he has submitted to the consideration of the House to-day, he confides the expenditure of a sum of over $6,500,000 to a company that has only put into that undertaking, so far as we can see, the sum of about $50,000, a company which is concentrated in the hands of a very few men, and they are charged with the expenditure of this sum of nearly $7,000,000 without any accountability to this House. According to the statement of my hon. friend, which of course we must take as well founded, it is the expectation that before long, if the transcontinental railway is going to be carried out, we shall take over that work, and it is going to become the property of the government. When I asked my hon. friend the acting Minister of Railways and Canals how soon he expected that would be done, he said that three years would be given to terminate the bridge. Under the expectation that the government are going to carry out that transcontinental railway as soon as possible, and if that bridge is terminated within three years, we will at that time, perhaps before, at any rate very soon after, under the general policy in connection with the transcontinental railway, be called upon to take up that work. So that we are confiding ihe construction of this bridge which we intend to make our own property, and the expenditure of a sum of over $6,500,000 to parties who are not responsible to the government. I say that we have no control over the spending of that money, no supervision, and that the interests of the city of Quebec and its vicinity, and the construction of that bridge and its approaches in such a way as to satisfy clearly the wants of the public at that point, are confided to a select few who form this company, without any accountability.
Clause 14, is the one under which this government is empowered to name three directors. But those directors are not obliged to make any report to the government, they are a minority in the board, and consequently that company that has a paid-up capital at the present moment of abbut $50,000-it 'is alleged $65,000-that company is going to have the spending of all this money and the carrying out of the work. Under these circumstances, the policy of the government being to see to the construction of that bridge, there being, as I understand it, no controversy about its utility, it seems to me it would have been far more proper for the government itself to undertake the construction of that bridge. My hon. friend may say that the government is only guaranteeing these bonds. But we must couple that statement with the statement made by the minister that we are going to take over that property, that it is a necessary link in the transcontinental railway, and I think-because I do not want to
go into the details, the calculations have been placed before this House by my hon. friend-but I think there can be no doubt in the mind of any member in this House that we are going ultimately to take up that property and make it a Dominion government property. Under these circumstances are we right to confide the spending of this money and the conduct of this undertaking, with its approaches to Quebec on one side and to Levis on the other, to a company concentrated in the hands of so few people, when it appears to be obvious that the control of that important undertaking and the progress of the work ought to be continually under the eyes of the government and under the eye of this parliament.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I find that that company lias not given conclusive proof of its competency to carry out an undertaking of that magnitude. Here let me call attention to a very important motion which was made before the legislature of Quebec by the member for Dorchester, in which the history of the operations of this company is fully gone into. The facts connected with the working of that company are enumerated in that motion, which I will not read to the House, but only point out some of the facts, and if those facts are correct, I submit that this scheme has been prepared hastily, at the last moments of the session, and that if the proposition which I lay before you is correct, it would be the duty of the government themselves to carry out these important works rather than to confide them to this company. At least I think we ought to have in this measure some provision whereby, from time to time and regularly, we should know, in the interests of the public, exactly how this money is being applied and how the works are being carried out. Let me call your attention to the fact that an estimate was prepared for the use of the Quebec government which then had control over this bridge, of what the bridge would cost. That estimate was prepared under the instructions of the then Minister of Public Works of the province of Quebec, the late Mr. Duffy, and on the 6th of August, 1902, was placed before the Quebec government.
Under the estimate made by a very careful engineer the cost of the substructure of this bridge was placed at $819,450, and the cost of the superstructure, after having been very carefully gone into by Mr. Yallee, the government engineer, was placed at $2,800.000. The province of Quebec subscribed to that undertaking the sum of $250,000 to be payable in instalments. That amount was to be paid to the builders of the bridge as the work proceeded. 20 per cent according to the estimates of work done on both substructure and superstructure and never more than $30,000 in one year. The amount granted by the city of Quebec was payable at once, and it was so paid. Under the conditions of the sub-

scription, although up to the present time the substructure alone is terminated, the province has already, as I understand it, paid $90,000 in cash, and- Mr. Parent, the provincial premier, who is also mayor of the city of Quebec and president of the bridge company, in spite of the conditions of the subscription of the province of Quebec, has, as president of the bridge company, pledged the province of Quebec to a loan made by the Bank of Montreal of $160,000. So that, although the bridge is not advanced in degree sufficient to authorize the total payment of the provincial subsidy to the structure, the whole of the subsidy under the management of this company, has become pledged to the company, and the whole amount is practically paid already.
Is that in addition to the amount of subsidy already paid ?

That is in addition to the $90,000 already paid. The contractor for the construction of the bridge is obliged, under the contract which he made with the bridge company, to pay for the construction of the bridge and for all contingencies and expenses of the company, whatever that may mean, with the federal subsidy, with the subsidy of the city of Quebec and also with the subsidy of the province, so that in reality it is he who lias disbursed up to the present time all the amounts connected with the construction of this bridge. The substructure has been finished. The cost was estimated by a competent engineer at $819,000, and yet we find by a document produced before the legislative assembly of Quebec, bearing No. 37 of the documents filed during the last session, that the amount due to this contractor for construction as far as it has progressed is not $819,000, but $1,217,359.38. On the one hand, an estimate made by Mr. Vallee, a competent engineer, of a little over $800,000 for the work to be done; on the other hand, an amount of expense incurred for the bridge so far of over $1,200,000. This claim of $1,200,000 due to the contractor has been approved by the company. That is a fact which we know. The company has also approved of an account due to the contractor for the beginning of the work done upon the superstructure of $199,000. These two items united form a total amount of expenditure due now by the company of $1,416,394. That is the amount due now, although, as far as I know, there is no superstructure yet upon the substructure and the substructure was valued at $819,000. In the Quebec legislature an effort was made to obtain some light upon this extraordinary expenditure, and a motion was made there having for its object the placing before the legislature of the details of all these claims, and notably of the moneys which the contractor, being liable for all contingent expenses, had paid to the law firm in' Quebec of which Mr. Parent, the

Prime Minister, is a member, in connection with the construction of this bridge. The legislature denied that motion upon thte supposed ground that in the Public Works Department at Quebec there could be found no information upon that, important point, the object of the motion, which was made on 11th March last, being to find out how It could be possible that such a large indebtedness as an amount of over $1,400,000 could have been incurred upon the undertaking which had advanced to such a point only as would warrant the expenditure of say $1,000,000 or almost $500,000 more than this work was valued at. T mention this fact to give the House some idea of how the work was carried on.
