Up to the present we have an expenditure upon the substructure of $1,217,000, which should have cost, according to the estimate of the engineer, $819,000, and an expenditure of $199,035 on the superstructure, making $1,416,394, part of which has been paid with the discount obtained at the Bank of Montreal, of the amount which was payable by the province of Quebec, 20 per cent of which was to have been paid as the work progressed, and not more than $30,000 in any one year.
Of the debentures of the company, as I understand it, $533,594 have been issued in payment of part of this construction account. With half a million of debentures they have paid indebtedness due on construction account to the amount of $213,258. Surely there has been a profit to somebody upon these debentures ? There was a sum of $213,258, or thereabouts, payable, and there was a sum of $188,721. which is the amount of the discount at the Bank of Montreal. At any rate, the debentures having been paid for at the rate of 60 per cent of their face value will yield a profit to somebody. At the present moment, the city of Quebec has paid $300,000, the province of Quebec has paid $250,000. and the Dominion government, on account of the $1,000,000 vote on account of this undertaking, has paid $374,533, or there has been a total on account of subsidies paid of $924,533.
When Mr. Yallee, the engineer of the provincial government, was commissioned by the Hon. Mr. Duffy, provincial treasurer, to make an accurate report upon the cost of these works, he reported the cost to be $819,000 for the substructure, and $2,800,000 for the superstructure. The estimate we have now before us and which was made in September last by Mr. Schreiber, brings the cost up to $4,767,500, or $1,148,050 more thau Mr. Yallee said the cost would be. We have no accurate information as to the cost of the approaches beyond what is contained in the estimate of Mr. Schreiber, and that estimate is very unsatisfactory because we do not know on what it is based. For the south approach, the estimate is $21,000 for land and damages, and $459,800 for the construction of the double track and a yard (presumably at Levis). The land and

damages estimated tor the north approach is much larger, being $414,000. We have no information as to what this estimate is based on, as to its details or as to whether it is correct. For the construction of tlie double tracks and the sidings the estimated sum is $533,060. The total amount in the estimate of Mr, Sehreiber up to the 17th of September as to the amount necessary to completely finish the undertaking is $(>,725,360. The debentures which will l>o issued by this company, and the control of the proceeds of which will be entirely in the hands of the company amount to $6,678,500. The estimated cost, as 1 have said is, $6,725,360. I would ask the Minister of Railways and Canals or the Minister of Justice, if it is intended to repay the province of Quebec and the city of Quebec with the proceeds of these bonds. The amount of subsidies given so far is $900,000 and that has gone into the construction of tlie work.
My hon. friend is omitting the duty.
I have omitted it purposely, because the steel rails may be made in Canada.
It is not for the steel rails. It is for the superstructure of the bridge which is being made in the United States at the present moment.
Even so, I do not think the figures meet the amount paid by the Dominion government, by the provincial government, and by the city of Quebec.
Absolutely.

I may say that so far the work has not been carried on by the company in a manner which would warrant us in believing that the company is more competent to carry out the work than is this government. From the papers submitted, to the House, it will be seen that probably four or five individuals control the whole company. What they have paid in so far they will have returned in paid up stock, and they are asked to invest a further sum of $200,000, but they will do so with a certain prospect that the government is going to take over the bridge, and they will receive five per cent upon the investment, plus ten per cent bonus, when the government takes over the whole undertaking. Under these circumstances, I feel that although the project is an excellent one; the people of the Dominion who are now interested in that work since it has become a national undertaking, and the people of the immediate district as well, would have far better security if the government had direct supervision over the expenditure of this six and a half million dollars. Since a commission is to be appointed for the express purpose of building the Transcontinental Railway, a part of which this bridge will become, it is my opinion that every interest would be far better safeguarded if the work were entrusted to that commission. I believe that the people in the vicinity of Quebec would prefer that this expenditure shall be under government control, through this commission of experienced men, so that they would have absolute knowledge of how every cent of this money would be spent. If we take the facts set forth in the motion made in the legislature, and the facts contained in the documents submitted to us here; there can be no controversy but that a great saving of money would be effected if the construction of this work were carried out. by the commission, or under tlie direct supervision of the Dominion government. We would thus secure absolute control of a work which is ultimately going to fall into the assets of the Dominion, which is part of a railway which has been sanctioned by parliament. If it was deemed necessary and useful to commit the construction of that railway to an independent body or a quasi independent body, to a commission composed of competent men, why should an exception be made of the Quebec bridge 7 Why should not that large sum of $6,500,000 which we are ultimately going to pay-we have that admission from the Minister of Finance, and there is no doubt about it in the mind of anybody-be confided to the same body, with such a control over the expenditure by this legislature as would ensure the money being spent in such a way as not to afford an opportunity for any company or individual to derive any profit from the carrying out of the undertaking, but to ensure the largest possible measure of public benefit.

Mr. Speaker, It is very pleasant indeed to hear my hon. friend admitting the absolute necessity of this undertaking. In fact, it would be impossible for any man with any knowledge of the local conditions existing at Quebec, to doubt, not merely the advisability, but the imperative necessity of the construction of such a work. For the last twenty-five years it has been the dream of every man in Quebec to see this work accomplished. We labour there under exceptional disadvantages. There are three important railways on the south side of the St. Lawrence- the Intercolonial, the Quebec Central and the Grand Trunk-none of which have connection with Quebec ; and a population of half a million people in a district tributary to Quebec are completely cut off from access to the city, except by means of a ferry, on which the rate in summer is two cents per 100 pounds, and in the winter four cents per 100 pounds. These rates are relatively prohibitive. It is gratifying to observe that the criticism of my hon. friend has reference not to the scheme, but to the method in which assistance is to be given to the eom-

pany. His chief criticism is with respect to the organization of the company itself. I am sure that my hon. friend must be labouring under a complete misapprehension when he imagines for one moment that the men connected with this company are liable in any way to divert any of the money they receive, or to be parties to an expenditure that is not absolutely necessary in the interest of the enterprise. It will suffice for me to give the names of the gentlemen who are connected with it. Take, for instance, the names of Mr. Chateauvert, Mr. Lemoine, Mr. Audet, Mr. Garneau, Mr. Breaky, Mr. Boswell, Mr. Laliberte, Mr. Rioux, Mr. Price. These are the names of the most prominent citizens of the city of Quebec ; and when my hon. friend learns that these men are directors of the company and are in control of it, he will realize the absolute impossibility of any such eventuality as that which he suggests occur-ing. My hon. friend will be glad to learn also that new capital is to be brought into this enterprise. I am sure that he will be pleased when I tell him that I am authorized to say that of this new stock of !i>200,000, Mr. John Sharpies, of Quebec, takes $50,000, the Allan firm, Mr. Hearn and others, $25,000, the Grand Trunk Company, $25,000, and the Quebec Central Company, $25,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: If my hon. friend will allow me, I do not think these men are very heroic. If I had money to invest at 5 per cent, with a 10 per cent premium, I should be quite willing to put it into that company.

I am pointing out the absolute impossibility of such eventualities as my hon. friend suggests occuring, with such men at the head of the enterprise. My hon. friend practically says that the directors are not to be trusted. What benefit have they to derive from the enterprise ? They are putting their own money into it, and what position do they occupy under this contract 7 Not one dollar's worth of work can be done without the approval of the government. Every plan and specification has to be submitted to the government.

Plans have to be approved of by the government, as in the case of every public work of that nature ; but they make the contracts, and they have absolute powers in regard to the location and construction of the work.

Let my hon. friend just read the last part of paragraph 6, of the contract, and he will find that the proceeds of the bonds are to remain in the possession of the government that the money is to be paid out on progress estimates, that the certificates of the work as it progresses must be made by the government engineer. What greater control could the government have ? If my hon. friend will read this contract, he will see Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
that the result of it is that this is a government work, carried on for the government through the agency of these men whose names I have mentioned. Not a dollar's worth of work can be done without the approval of the government, not a toll can be levied or a farthing charged except with the consent of the government. What more direct control could there be ?
Is the contract already let for the completion of the bridge and the approaches ?

Yes, it was let years ago ; and if my hon. friend will look at the contract, he will see that provision was made fixing the price of the iron at the time that it should be required- a very important provision ; because as the result of that we have saved the consequences of fluctuations in the iron market, and are able to contract with the company under very favourable conditions. The contracts both for the superstructure and for the approaches have been submitted to the government engineer.
Were they submitted before they were signed '?
Yes, before they were executed.
Has the Phoenix Bridge Company the contract for the superstructure ?
Yes.
What is the amount of the contract for the superstructure 1
Three million three hundred and eighty-eight thousand three hundred dollars for the steel part, $156,500 for the wooden part, and $4,800 for the track on the bridge.
Are all these contracts with the same company ?
Yes, they are all in the one contract.
What is the length of the bridge ?

I cannot give the length. I know that the centre span, the cantilever span, will be something like 1,800 feet in length. It will be close on 200 feet longer than the span of the bridge of the Frith of Forth, which at present is the largest span in the world.
What is its length in miles, in a general way ?
I imagine it would be a mile from the abutment on the north side to the shore abutment on the south side. Of course, the expensive part of the bridge will be the cantilever portion ; the centre span.

Does the hon. gentleman know whether the cost of the substructure exceeded1 the estimate, owing to the difficulty of finding a proper foundation ? I understand that the contractor had to go down a greater depth than he at first anticipated.

That is the cost of the superstructure already existing, but I would like to say that the estimate made by the provincial government engineer in that connection does not happen to agree with the estimate made by the Dominion government engineer. There was over $300,000 extra expenditure as the result of the discovery, when the south pier was put down, that it was practically on quicksand, which made it necessary to go down some 15 or 18 feet deeper than was originally contemplated. I may say that the estimate of the work done is not an approximate estimate, such as is made before a work is begun. The figures now submitted are based on the work actually done and approved by the Dominion government engineer. In so far as the subsidy granted by the Dominion government is concerned, it was neeesssary that the progress estimates of the work done each month should be approved by the Dominion government engineer before any subsidy could be paid, so that the figures given here are not an estimate made by Mr. Vallee, who may or may not be a competent man, and who may or may not have seen works of this magnitude carried on before, but they are an estimate of the actual work done.
My hon. friend has referred to the estimate of the cost of the approaches. He says that we have not sufficient detail. But it is a very easy matter to make an estimate of the cost of the approaches. The first question to be considered is the question of land damages; and any one who has any knowledge of the conditions in the neighbourhood of Quebec can easily determine the probable cost of the land grants. The whole territory covered by the approaches on the north side of the river will not exceed six miles, and it is very easy to estimate within that distance what the cost of the land is likely to be. The next question is what is the cost of construction likely to be, that is to say, the embankment, the grading and the iron. But that is all very simple. There is no great trouble making an estimate of that description, and in any event we have the statement made by Mr. Schreiber. the government engineer, on whose experience we may safely rely.
How is the approach made on the north side of Quebec ?

The approach starts from the north abutment of the bridge and goes down along the river front, extending to the city of Quebec and ending in a place called Champlain market,
at which point the existing railway systems -the Great Northern and the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Lake St. John-will connect with the contemplated terminus.
Is that near the dock which the government built ?
About a quarter of a mile from it. The point I speak of now is immediately below the Dufferin Terrace.
Does it go around the bank of the river ?

Yes. The result will be you will not only have a bridge at Quebec, but material for the best harbour in the world. You will have six miles of river front served by this line of railway, and you will have 42 feet of water over the whole course, with a very small expenditure. Instead of being, as now, absolutely dependent upon the Princess Louise Basin, where you have got but two berths for steamers drawing 30 feet of water, yon will have this whole river front covered by this line of railway. Not only are we now providing for a bridge to connect the north side of the St. Lawrence with the south, but also for the harbour improvements; because when you get down towards the city of Quebec to within about a mile of the terminus, you then run along the wharfs, and it will be necessary to build an embankment along the wharfs, which will afterwards serve as' a magnificent embankment for sea-going vessels. You are not only providing this means of communication between the north and south shores, but further equipping the harbour of Quebec, so that you can have then a most commodious and complete harbour.
How is it contemplated to get down from the height of the abutment of the bridge on the north side to the level of Champlain market ?

According to the profile now in existence, it is intended to start from the upper level of Cap Rouge, then go along the cliff to get down to the lower level at Pointe a. Pizeau, immediately below Sillery church. There you will reach the lower level, and from Pointe fl. Pizeau there will be an approach of three and a half miles into the city on absolutely level ground.
I had an idea that the fortification went sheer down to the water.

No, but the government property does. The natural fortification does. The basis of the citadel goes down to the water ; but at the (base of the rock on which the citadel is built, there is a narrow piece of ground where the Allans wharf is situated.
How broad ?
About 100 feet, and then you immediately come to the water.
Sufficient for a harbour and the transaction of business ?
Yes, there is not a single house in that locality. My hon. friend will remember that that is where the landslide took place some years ago, and there have been no houses there since.
That is what gave me the impression that there is no room fox-wharfs there.
Yes, there is. That is where the Allans formerly brought their vessels to discharge and take on passengers. There are about 25 to 30 feet of water there, and out from the wharf we have 40 to 50 feet.
Will the x-ailway track run along this narrow strip ?

Yes, the intention is to run by that place and down to the terminus, which is about a quarter mile further down. My hon. friend made refex-ence to the contribution of the city of Quebec and that of the province, and asked how they ought to be dealt with ? When that enterprise was started, the city of Quebec voted $300,000 to aid it, and the provincial legislature, realizing- 'that it was a work of provincial importance, voted it a sum of $250,000. With respect to that $250,000, my hon. friend m-ade reference to something that occurred in the local legislature, and said that I probably knew all about it. Well, I know very little aboixt what takes place there. We have as much as we can take care of here, without paying attention to what goes on in the legislature at Quebec. But I do know something of this transaction. The $200,000 was voted in aid of the construction of this bridge, payable at the rate of $30,000 per year, but if before the total amount of $200,000 would be paid at that x-ate, the work should be completed, then the total amount would become payable at once. As the work progressed rapidly, the money was eax-ned very rapidly. The substructure was begun and completed within two years.
I am now speaking in the hearing of the chief engineer of the government, and I say it is acknowledged and admitted that there is no more perfect piece of work on this continent than the work which has been done in connection with the sub-stx-ucture. The -work was all completed within two years, the provincial contribution of $250,000 was earned but was not available because, under the contx-act, the money payable by the provincial government and by the city of Quebec was payable pro rata on each progress estimate. The money was very x-apidly eax-ned but was not available because under the terms of the Mr. GOURLEY.
statute it was payable to the amount of only $30,000 a year. In order to enable them to meet their obligations and to pay their contractor, the company went to the bank of Montreal and the bank of Montreal advaix-ced the money, taking as collateral security this $250,000 due from the province ; that is the whole transactioix. The province agreed to pay $30,000 a year and instead of paying the contractor they pay the bank which advances the money. My hon. friend x-eferred to the advances of the city and province. In so far as the city and province are concerned, I may say that the city is much interested in the construction of the bridge and that the $300,000 which they have contributed was contributed as a voluntary gift with the intention that th'e shareholders of this company should benefit to that extent. That is the intention. I have here the resolution of the city council of Quebec in which they say that this is intended as aid to the enterprise. They did not expect any part of this money to be returned. The province of Quebec gave their contribution as a subsidy absolutely, as the Dominion government agreed to give $1,000,000 and have paid $374,000. Thxis you have the Dominion, the province axxd the city all realizing that this is an important work municipally, px-ovincially and from a Dominion standpoint and they all contributed to the work. Now it comes to pass that possibly the work may be taken over, under this agreement, by the Dominion. That is to say that one of the parties who contributed to the -construction of the enterprise may take the whole enterprise over at a certain time. If the Dominion should take it over and px-ovide for the expenditure they are called upon to make under the existing contx-act, [DOT] then this will happen : After the Dominion has been released of ail obligations with respect to the bonded indebtedness or the sinking fund for the amount paid to the shareholders, on their stock, then you will have the Dominion interested in this enterprise to the extent of $370,000, the amount of the subsidy. You will have tiie province of Quebec interested to the extent of $250,000 and the city of Qxiebee to the extent of $300,000. Then the Dominion says : After we have been relieved from all liabilities under the new arrangement, and after we go back to the old condition of things, then we shall deal with this entex1-prise as an enterprise in which three parties are interested ; and after we get rid of all our obligations, if there is any px-oflt, we do not want to take the profit, we are not entitled to it any more than the others who contributed to the enterprise. Then all of those who put money into the enterprise will receive their money back. The gov-enxment will have the right either to pay back the capital or to keep the money in the enterprise and pay the province and city so much per cent per annum

oil their investment. It seems to me that that is a perfectly fair proposition and one which places all those who have put money into this project on the same footing. I do not know that there is any thing in what my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) would criticise.

I did not make any particular criticism of that, but if my hon. friend will allow me, 1 will read the resolution to which I referred. The resolution says :
On the 10th of August, Mr. Vallee, the engineer of the provincial government reported that out of the $250,000 to be paid by the province to the company. $56,600.45 would have to be allotted to the substructure and $195,399.55 to the superstructure. On the 21st of September following the Order in Council was passed adopting the conclusions of this report and in spite of the fact that the payment of the subsidy has been divided, although, the superstructure alone was constructed the province have paid already $90,000 instead of $56,000. Moreover, on the 4th of December following, the Minister of Public Works made a report the object of which was to contradict the Order in Council of September 21, 1900, in which report of the September 21st, it was declared that the whole $250,000 was then fully earned and that the government of the province of Quebec should bind and oblige itself to pay that sum of $250,000 to the Bank of Montreal in contradiction to the Premier's Order in Council and although the work was not completed and the conditions of the grant by the province had not been observed.

If my hon. friend will look at the statute he will see that It has been literally complied with. I am not dealing with the motion, because motions can be so easily made to read so as to suit a particular purpose. I refer to the statute of the province which provides for the subsidy and my hon. friend will find that the transfer to the Bank of Montreal was made literally under the terms of that statute.
Another error into which my hon. friend has fallen is the. statement that nothing has been done in connection with the superstructure There has been expended on the superstructure the modest sum of $156,000 ; two short spans have been completed and are now in place and can he seen by any one who passes by the bridge. $156,640 have been expended in connection with the superstructure. The subsidy of the province of Quebec has simply been transferred. It is paid over to those who have earned it, and it has gone into the enterprise, there is no dispute about that and it has gone in on progress estimates certified by Mr. Vallee the government engineer who certifies to the payment of progress estimates by the province of Quebec. My hon. friend has referred to the motion of Mr. Pelletier, I would like to refer to something which occured in the city of Quebec about two nights ago when my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) and his leader (Mr. Borden, Halifax) were entertained in that city and it was a great pleasure to me to observe that when
the gentleman went to Quebec that city maintained its reputation for hospitality and that a magnificent reception was given to him. I congratulate him. The gentleman who made that motion, speaking of the bridge at the banquet in the hearing of my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) said :
The Quebec bridge has been promised to us by important Conservatives. That promise was not kept, and that was an error. The electors should always insist upon the accomplishment of any promises made and they should prefer that fewer promises he made and that those made be carried out.
Mr. Pelletier did not say that that promise was not kept by the present administration and like my hon. friend he approves of the building of the bridge.
Not of this proposition ; lie did not know anything about this.

No ; that motion in the Quebec legislature to which my hon. friend refers was probably made for the purpose of making party capital, but I am glad to see that here we are broader and do not try to make political capital out of a public enterprise.
I do not know that there is anything more for me to say at this stage hut when we are in committee If there are any questions which hon. gentlemen desire to ask and which I can answer I shall be glad to answer them. I may say to my hon. friend that I have a very great interest in this bridge.
Not a financial one ?
Not to the extent of a farthing, direct or indirect and I do not think any one suspects me of having an interest.
No, I did not say so. You have too much sense.

This goes into my constituency, into the heart of one of the most important parishes I represent, my native parish Sillery. It goes through a part of the county with which I am very familiar and runs down to the constituency of my hon. friend for Quebec West (Mr. Power) and both of us are much interested, for as I said, for a quarter of a century the dream of every man in Quebec was to see this bridge built. It was promised and promised, to us but we never saw the realization of it. We have now come within, I think, measurable distance of the end. I have made myself familiar, as far as I could with the abilities I possess, with all the particulars of the enterprise and I assure this 'honourable House that any information I can give I shall be glad and delighted to give.
With respect to the discount on the bonds I may say that this is the position : When this contract was let the company had, as paid up capital. $50,000. It had available for the construction of this bridge, subsidies

of the Dominion government, of the local 'government, and of the city of Quebec. That is to say, $300,000 from the city of Quebec, $250,000 from the provincial government, -and $333,000 from the Dominion government, for there was then available out of the Dominion subsidy for the substructure only on-e-third, and more than that has been paid out of that Dominion subsidy in connection with the superstructure. That was the financial condition of the company at that time. Now, this contractor entered into a contract with this company to build that work, a most important undertaking. As 1 say, at that time no man knew what the result of this undertaking might be with respect to the foundation. They have been obliged to put in this foundation sixty feet below the bed of the St. Lawrence river, at a place where the tide rises eighteen feet. At times his men were working at a distance of thirty-two feet below the surface of the water.
What is the tide at that place ?
It varies from fourteen to eighteen feet.

The Shubenacadie bridge was built in forty feet of water.
The MINISTER OB' JUSTICE. The conditions under which the Shubenacadie bridge was built did not at all compare with those prevailing here. Those were the conditions under which the contract was taken, and this contractor agreed to take 80 per cent of his progress -estimates in cash and 20 per cent in bonds of the company-one-fifth of the whole cost of the substructure in bonds of the company, and the company in the financial condition I have described. Now what was the outlook for him at that time ? Was the outlook such as that he could ever expect under these conditions, if lie did not take considerable risk, even to receive the payment of 60 cents on the dollar ? There was large risk, and he took that risk, and the result has been that the enterprise has turned out a success. Now lie says, I want a hundred cents on the dollar, that is the condition of the contract. Now what position does the government take ? The government says : This is a binding obligation on the company. The company undertook at that time to enter into a contract and to assume this binding obligation. They agreed to pay that 40 cents on the dollar, it is an obligation that can be enforced against the company at any time. The government say to the company : Yery well

What was the object of the company to pay the difference ?
The MINISTER OB' JUSTICE. The position the government took was this : The government said : Yery well, that is a binding obligation, a legal obligation that may be enforced against the company,1

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: and they must provide the means necessary to pay that obligation. Provide the means necessary to pay that obligation, subscribe an additional $200,000, which will be sufficient to pay that discount of $183,000, let the company pay that, and then when the company has liquidated that liability to its contractor and paid that discount, we will step in and guarantee their bonds, but we won't do it until the company have paid the difference. That is the position the government took. I do not see that there is anything wrong in that. It is merely providing that the company should liquidate its own liabilities with respect to that particular contractor. The company is asked to liquidate this liability, and in the result we have the additional guarantee that the construction of this enterprise will be properly looked after, because of the additional investment that these gentlemen are going to make in the enterprise, they are putting $200,000 more of their own capital into the -enterprise. The hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has this in his mind, that if the government take this enterprise over, of course the shareholders will be paid the $200,000. But the government will not take this enterprise over if it is not a success, the government are under no obligation to take it over.
They can do it.

But they are under no obligation to do it, and the government will see to it that this enterprise is not taken over if it becomes a financial disaster ; but if it. becomes a success, and if the government do take it over, why should we not assume this liability as well as any other liability ? If it is a legal obligation, a fair and honest debt due by the company, why should it not be paid ?
Can you do this without coming to this parliament and getting a grant of that money ?
We could not get it of course without the sanction of parliament, and we make that provision.
Under the contract you are empowering the government to enter into an arrangement of that kind. If you have -entered into an arrangement, the question is whether you will not be bound by that.
We would have to come to parliament for the money to do it.
But it. may be obligatory upon the Crown.

This is a provision which will enable the government as against the company to exercise its rights. But that does not mean that if parliament does not sanction the act of the government

they can do it. If parliament does not give its sanction there is no obligation.
We are empowering the government to enter into an arrangement of that kind if they think proper.

Let my hon. friend read section 23 :
It at any time, and with or without notice, the government shall pay or cause to be paid to the government of the province of Quebec and the city of Quebec, or either of them, the amount of their respective subsidies of $250,000, and $300,000, all payments, whether in respect of capital or income, to be made under the foregoing provisions to the said government of the province of Quebec or the city of Quebec, respectively, shall at and from that time absolutely cease and determine.
We are under no obligation to pay them anything. This is a provision that if we do pay them that, in order to get rid of even a moral claim, they may possibly have, that we shall pay them this amount with the interest mentioned in the clause. There is no other obligation upon us to do it

I would like to ask if the government have considered the claim made by the city of Montreal for aid to the Lon-gueuil bridge, In connection with this matter.
The MINISTER OF JUSTICE, I am under the impression that the company that was incorporated for the Longueuil bridge has no legal existence, I do not think that a company was ever formed. The Incorporation Act was passed, but I do not think that the companay ever took any action under it. Let me remind the hon. gentleman that this is not a local matter. Let me also remind him that there are at Montreal and in the immediate vicinity three bridges across the St. Lawrence.
Private bridges.

Very private. Look at the estimates of what they have cost the country, and you will find that the country is largely interested in them. There is the Victoria bridge, the La-chine bridge and the bridge 'at Coteau, and now we are- providing this session for the Bout be l'lle bridge.
That does not cross the St. Lawrence river.

I think the House will agree that this is a very necessary work in carrying out the general transportation scheme. But while this is the case, there is certainly some difference of opinion as to the manner in which this scheme is being carried out. The hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) 'did not clear up all the difficulties which I discovered on looking through this contract as it appears before ns. In the first place, there seems to be no accounting for the amount of stock, of which a great deal has
been made, that is supposed to have been paid up by the company. In looking over the estimates as given us in the preamble of the agreement, and also in the letters of Premier Parent, in connection with this matter, I find that the amount paid out to the contractor on account of the work done is exactly equal, with the exception of a difference of $56, to the amount of the subsidies which have been received, so that no part of the capital stock of the company has gone into construction, and I fail to understand where the capital has gone.

There was a great deal of preliminary work before the contract was entered into at all. There was no more difficult engineering work to be done anywhere than in connection with the location of the bridge.

That is all taken into consideration in the estimates we have from the Department of Railways and Canals, and yet the amount paid out of the capital stock remains unaccounted for. I fail to see why the government should be called upon to guarantee or to make the company guarantee 100 cents on the dollar in the payment of these bonds. The contractor took them at 60 cents on the dollar in payment for work done. These bonds are drawing interest at their full face value of 100 cents on the dollar, so that the contractor has made a very good bargain with the company. The difference between $283,279, Which the bonds realized, and the $472,000, which is the face value of the bonds, is $188,000. It would follow that $283,000, being the amount which the contractor gave the company credit for, this $188,000 is an amount which may be called the water of these bonds. The government by this process are performing1 a modern miracle ; they are turning water into gold instead of turning it into wine. It seems to me that this is a matter with which the government should have nothing to do, and that it is a matter which should be settled by the contractor and the bridge company. I notice that the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals estimates the total cost of this bridge at $6,725,360, and I must congratulate the deputy minister upon the way in which his estimate coincides with ' the amount of the contract. The hon. Minister of Justice tells us that the amount of the contract for the steel superstructure is $3.388,800. That is exactly the amount of the estimate of the deputy minister for that work. The hon. Minister of Justice tells us that the contract for the wooden floor beams is $156,500. That also coincides exactly with the estimate of the deputy minister. The hon. Minister of Justice tells us that the contract for the track on bridge is $4,800, exactly coinciding with the estimate of the deputy minister. We find then that $6,725,360 is the estimated cost of this work, an estimate which, as I say, agrees exactly
147] 9

with the contract. There has been paid for this work in cash, the .proceeds of the subsidies, $914,862, which leaves a balance of $5,811,000, which, according to the estimate, will be the amount required to complete the bridge. But Mr. Parent, president of the Bridge Company, and Premier of the province of Quebec, has requested that $6,900,000 of the bonds be guaranteed in order to complete the bridge. The government have not seen fit to accede to the whole of his request, but 'they have agreed to guarantee bonds to the amount of $6,678,200. That leaves an apparent difference of something like $1,000,000. That is attempted to be accounted for by the duty on the steel superstructure. I presume that the contract is given for the steel superstructure. The estimate is placed at three and a half cents per pound, which is a fair price at the present time for heavy bridge material. If it were lighter bridge material, it would probably amount to three and three-quarter cents a pound. It is not proper to add the duty to the cost of construction of the bridge. That is already accounted for in the contract price, and at any rate the steel should be bought in Canada. There is a million of difference in that, and there is $188,000, the difference between the amount which the bonds realized on their face value, which have not been accounted for. The members of this House are all agreed as to the necessity for this bridge and that the work is one which should be done in carrying out the general transportation scheme of this country and providing the necessary transportation facilities for the great trade development which is going on. For anything which is going to a national undertaking I am perfectly willing to vote any necessary amount, but I do think that this scheme as proposed is not a proper one. We know something about these bridge matters in the province of New Brunswick, from which I come. There is just such another bridge, only a cheaper bridge, in the city of St. John, owned by a bridge company, and built by the bridge company just as this bridge is being built at Quebec. It was built under the old government. Almost the entire amount of the money used in construction was loaned by the government, as I understand it, and upon it they paid a certain rate of interest- I think 4 per cent or 4J per cent. I am not sure as to the details of the undertaking, but the members of the government will know them. As a matter of fact, that bridge company have made a splendid revenue out of that bridge, although the amount of money they put into the bridge was very small. I ain told on the best authority that every year the stockholders in that bridge company receive actually more than double the amount they put in. I have understood -I do not vouch for the accuracy of these figures-that the actual amount paid in by each stockholder was $700, and that each
year they have an income from the bridge of $1,100 or $1,200. 'That is done at the expense of the general public. Certainly a handicap and a hindrance to trade are caused by allowing these people to charge a greater amount for the carriage of trade over this bridge than should be allowed.
They can-hot do it here.

The conditions in this case, I do not think, are different from the conditions of the other. I think the conditions in both cases are about alike. The government should build this bridge themselves. They are actually undertaking all the risk of this enterprise. They are guaranteeing, not only the interest, but they are absolutely guaranteeing the principal of the bonds ; they are guaranteeing the whole amount, and if there is any profit the company will reap the benefit of it. It is shown here, if we are to believe the estimate of receipts, that there is going to be a fine thing in this for the company. The expectation is that they will be able to divide $56,000 a year on the lowest estimate of profit. After they pay interest on the bonds and after they provide for the wear and tear and other expenses of maintenance, they will still have a profit of $56,000. They actually pay in $200,000. and the amount of $65.000, which the hon. Minister of Justice says was put into preliminary work, or $265,000 in all, and they divide a profit of $56,000, which is a pretty nice income from an investment of $265,000. That is equal to 25 or 30 per cent.
The government has no liability at all.

It has been presented to us as an essential feature of the scheme, that it is a profitable scheme and that the government will not incur liability. There are contingencies which might throw liability on the government, and so far the government are incurring the only liability in the whole case. They are not only guaranteeing the bonds to be issued but they are actually guaranteeing at least sixty jrer cent of the bonds already issued by the company. There is no responsibility whatever upon the company; with them it is a ease of heads I win tails you lose. Why do not the government do the work themselves, when they can do it better and more economically.
If it is not a success and the government does not r take it over, what becomes of the $200,000 of new money that is to be invested ?
The Minister of Justice quite understands that it would be a very easy matter to provide $200,000 without a cent being put up.
Oh, no.
I do not say that it will be done in this case, but there are instances on record where it has been done and I could tell the hon. gentleman how it could be done.
Don't.

I will not, because in case the Minister of Justice does not know, if I told him perhaps he would communicate it to the company and I want to avoid that. We are assuming all the responsibility, and if the bridge is not a success we are the losers. While I am very strongly in favour of the building of this bridge, and while I believe it will be as beneficial as the Minister of Justice thinks, and will enable the harbour of Quebec to get trade in increasing quantities which we would all be glad to see; yet I cannot but think that it would be much better for the government to build the bridge under the Railway Commission, or by a special commission, believing as I do that it would then be built in a more economic manner, and that the money of the country would not be wasted.
it cannot build one single foot of wharf. If the Minister of Justice will refer to the records of the Public Works Department he will find that it will cost about $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 to provide proper accommodation at the very place he has spoken of. 'there is a batture right opposite-

The hon. gentleman must know the Mariners' Chapel at the immediate entrance to Diamond Harbour. From Diamond Harbour down to the Champlain Market there will be three-quarters of a mile where you are absolutely on the shore of the river. You have to go along on the wharfs with your railway, you cannot go anywhere else. There is no use talking about a batture.
I know that, but the Minister of Justice knows as well as I do, and perhaps better, that there is a batture there which prevents ships from coming to the shore.
Not at all.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. I. TARTE (Montreal, St. Mary's).
speechtext: I was one of the promoters of the Quebec Bridge Company years ago, and I have always taken a great interest in this work. The country is now invited to guarantee $6,678,000 in addition to what we have contributed in the past. The Dominion treasurer has paid $374,000, the province of Quebec, $250,000; the city of Quebec, $300,000; in all, $924,000. If I understand the position, the contract for the substructure is the only contract that has been awarded. I do not exactly know the amount of the contract entered into with Mr. Davis, but the amount estimated by the chief engineer for the substructure is $1,217,400 and the cost of the superstructure, for which a contract has not yet been given, is estimated at $3,388,000. That will make $4,600,000 for the substructure and the superstructure of the bridge itself. The balance of the money which we are asked to guarantee is for land damages, construction of double track, tracks on the bridge, wooden floor, &c., the whole reaching the large sum of $7,500,000. About $1,000,000 is going to be employed in land and damages, and the purchase of land. I lived for fifteen'years very near the spot where the bridge is built, and I know the locality very well. The land on the north side belongs to private parties who will be very glad indeed to sell it. There is to be $414,000 for land and damages on the north side, and a little more for the south side. The Minister of Justice has said that the government is providing at the same time six miles of water front accommodation. Well, the new project, as it is placed before us to-day, will not provide for one foot of water front accommodation in Quebec. There is no money voted for deep water wharfs, and with the amount of money placed at the disposal of the company to purchase land, 461
Yes.
Why, the batture begins at the upper end of Lamp-son's cove and goes up to Sillery.

Surely the Minister of Justice knows that the bridge is being built at Cap Rouge, much further up than Sillery. The bridge is being built at Cap Rouge; and I say that to give proper water accommodation in those six miles would involve an expenditure of $10,000,000. There are reports in the Department of Public Works to show this.
What have the improvements at Montreal cost, and what length of water front is there ?

There is no possible comparison between the two. I speak of the Quebec case as I know it to be. My hon. friends have only to look at the expenditure provided for here. There is not one cent for wharf accommodation. The money is provided for the purchase of land, for the building of sheds, stations, and so on, for the bridge itself, and for the approaches on both sides of the river ; but not one foot of water accommodation is provided for. This point I think I have made very clear, and it cannot be disputed by anybody who knows.
As to the financial aspect of the project, it stands thus :	This government at first
agreed to give $1,000,000 of subsidy to the company, the Quebec government and the city of Quebec supplying the balance of the subsidies, which this very same company declared to be sufficient to carry out the undertaking. My hon. friends on both sides of the House have only to refer to the debates which have taken place in the Quebec House and also here, and to the reports



of the company, as proof of that fact. Well, the company have heen mistaken in their calculations. 1 do not blame them too much for that, because in the case of such large undertakings X quite admit that we are all liable to make mistakes. I know that Mr. Davis, in order to have safe foundations for his piers, has been obliged to go much deeper than he anticipated. Of course, he should have looked carefully into the nature of the soil at the bottom of the St. Lawrence before undertaking this contract. At the same time, not desiring to be unfair to him, 1 grant that that cost him a pretty large amount of money ; but it is only a detail. The two governments and the city of Quebec have already paid nearly $1,000,000. In my opinion, if the subsidies had been capitalized and if the undertaking had been floated in a business-like manner, there was enough money to carry out the work. Many able business men have expressed the same view. However, the project has not been carried out, and we have now to say whether or not we approve of the scheme placed before us. The government are to guarantee fifty-year bonds for over $0,000,000. If I understand the seventh clause of the contract, the government will issue these bonds as the company earn the money. In other words, the contractor will be paid by the company with the proceeds of the bonds as he earns the amounts so paid. I want to ask my hon. friends on the treasury benches whether this is a very good financial method. If the bonds were floated in one block

Look at paragraph 8. Provision is made first for getting the money. That is to be got in any way the government shall determine most advisable under the circumstances ; that is to say, by making one issue of the bonds at one time, or by making partial issues at different times. It would be premature to say now how that should be done.
The government holds the money and pays it out on progress estimates ?
Yes.
I would like the point to be made clear. Suppose the bonds are issued in one block, how is the money to be disposed of ?
It goes to the credit of the government, and will be paid out on monthly progress estimates ns the money is earned.

The Minister of Justice said a moment ago that the contract for the superstructure has not been awarded. What interest have the contractors to do work as cheaply as they can when they know that the government will take over the work ? The Minister of Finance has said that very distinctly. In my humble

opinion, the position in which we are placed is that we are giving without tender a contract to a contractor. The government have stated that the work is of a national character ; and having stated that, they will take it over, what is the use of our giving a guarantee of 3 per cent to a private company ? What is the use of leaving the whole thing in the dark ? Because we do not know whether the bonds will be floated In one block or in several small blocks ; that is a question to be decided. The only thing we are sure about is that we guarantee fifty-year debentures at 3 per cent interest. The money will be borrowed ou our own credit at 3 per cent. Under the circumstances, as some hon. members who have preceded me have said, would it not be better for us to take over the work now ? 1 do not see any reason why we should guarantee bonds at 3 per cent for private parties, undertaking at the same time to take over the work ; because there is no possible doubt that the government will take it over. There is one very clear reason that will oblige them to take it over, and very soon. I say all success to the (bridge, but I believe there is not much doubt that the work will not pay its working expenses and the 3 per cent at the beginning and for some years. This means that we will take over the work as soon as it is completed. Therefore I say again that we are only giving without tender a contract to the Quebec Bridge Company, and we are giving the guarantee of our national credit without having complete control over the work. In my humble opinion, the government would have done better if they had settled immediately with Mr. Davis and the company, and had taken over the work, and borrowed the money to complete it on the national credit, instead of borowing for the benefit of a private corporation. It is beyond question, and we cannot blame them, that the men expect to make a profit out of the transaction. If they were not expecting that, they would be fools indeed. They are in business to make money, and not for love ; but if it were not too late, and I do not think it is, and if the company were disposed to come to an agreement to that effect, I think it would be better for the government to carry out the work themselves. I am for the equipment of the port of Quebec, and I hope that this guarantee will not prevent the government from equipping that port at a later period. That is a greater necessity than the building of this bridge. The bridge will be a useful thing, works of that kind are always useful, but it will not bring to the city of Quebec one-tenth of the trade which would be brought by the proper equipment of the ports of Montreal, Three Rivers, Quebec and our lake and canal ports. In my humble opinion, the government should lose no time in making up their minds to complete the equipment of the St. Lawrence route.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. A. PRINGLE (Cornwall and Stormont).
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that an important measure of this kind should be brought down earlier in the session instead of being presented to us a day or two before prorogation. However, there seems to be a eon-sensus of opinion that the work would be of great benefit, not only to the province of -Quebee, dmbdo-thfr Dominion of Canada. If I remember rightly, two or three years ago the Quebec Bridge Company was incorporated; and in the letters of incorporation the government reserved full powers to control rates, as is usually done in cases of the kind. As I understand it, the city of Quebec gave a bonus of $300,000 to this com pany, all of which has gone into the enterprise; the province of Quebec gave $250,000, and the Dominion government has agreed to give $1,000,000, on which it has paid $374, 353. We find, therefore, that the company has received from the city, the province and the Dominion, $924,253. It has also received payments on capital stock amounting to $65,585.70, making total cash receipts of $889,938.70 already invested in the project, and the company now finds itself in this position, that it is not able to finance the balance of the scheme. It seems to me, Sir, that the position is such that the government has authority to come to the assistance of this company. If it should not, the company will not be able to go on with the construction of this work. I have listened attentively to what was said by a number of gentlemen who spoke on this question, and I quite understand the importance of having a bridge at that point. We find that there is no bridge east of Montreal,' and there is a distance of 180 miles which is practically closed during five months in the year, between the south and north shores, from Montreal to Quebec. West of Montreal we have the Canadian Pacific Railway bridge, the Canada Atlantic Railway bridge and the Ottawa and New York Railway bridge-three bridges spanning the St. Lawrence within a distance of some 07 miles. I can quite understand, therefore, the importance of having a bridge at the city of Quebec. The only question to my mind is whether this contract properly safeguards the public interest, and if I am wrong in any statement I may make, I should like to be corrected. I understand that on consideration of the government guaranteeing these bonds, amounting to $6,678,200, the company releases and foregoes all claim to the $625,647, being the balance due on the million dollar subsidy. Then, the hon. member for King's (Mr. Fowler) raised a question with regard to the stock As I understand the condition, there is $65, 000 worth of stock, or rather $55,000, paid up on the stock subscribed, and under section 3 the company agree with the subscrib ers to the capital stock, that they shall surrender such stock to the company, and in 461*
lieu thereof accept paid-up stock to that amount paid by them on their shares and be relieved from further liability on the stock so surrendered.
Section 4 provides for issue of stock to the extent of $200,000, the proceeds to be applied in payment of the discount at which the bonds of the company were issued.
So far as I am concerned, I quite conceive that the $472,000 are a legal liability, and shall have to be discharged, either by the company or by the government, if they assume this work, but it did seem to me that the wise and proper way would have been for the government simply to have guaranteed the bonds for an amount including the $472,000.
With regard to section 7, the hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) raised an objection. As I understand that section, the bonds guaranteed by the government shall be issued and the proceeds thereon paid to the company as the construction is proceeded with, to the satisfaction of the government, and in such sums as the chief engineer of the government railways, -or such other officer as the government may appoint, may certify or justify. How far do these words ' or justify ' go ? Would the engineer of the government have the right to inquire whether the amount paid was a proper one, having regard to the value of the work, and whether any contract was given at a greater amount than it should have been ? Would the government engineer be justified in inquiring into the value of the work done ? I think the public interest should be protected on that point. I do not wish to detain the House, but simply wish to understand thoroughly this matter, as it is important. I understand, of course, that under section 12 the plans and specifications have to be approved by the Governor in Council, and further, that the government will control the tolls. I understand it lies largely in the power of the government to fix the tolls.
Absolutely.

In that case, the government can fix the tolls at such a rate that they may.collect a revenue sufficient to pay 3 per cent interest on the $6,678,200, or $200.346. Judging by the reports we have, it appears to me that even at a moderate rate of tolls, there will be no difficulty in collecting an amount sufficient to pay the 3 per cent on the bonds guaranteed by the government. It seems to me that the position of the government is such, if it had to intervene and either take the works entirely out of the hands of the company or adopt some means such as the plan now submitted of seeing that the works were completed.

I am glad to see that my hon. friend from Corn-

[DOT]wall (Mr. Pringle) supports this motion. The support should come from other provinces. We have been accustomed to seeing a fight between the provinces when any measure was proposed that benefited any one province and I am glad to see the hon. member for Cornwall (Mr. Pringle) supporting this scheme. I read the contract thoroughly and as far as the terms are concerned it is [DOT]well enough, if there is nothing behind it. If the provisions here set forth are carried out there can be no harm in the transaction, but unfortunately the trouble with these schemes is that it so often happens that people suspect that some one is going to get boodle out of the project; that is the misfortune of our public life, the suspicion that there is some steal. In the past Canada has been divided into two parts by the River St. Lawrence, and in the old days had it been in Europe it would have been two countries; but now, with the construction of railways and the building of bridges, countries are united that in the old days would be separate and I say that this bridge should have been built years ago. Quebec should have been united and as a maritime province man I have always felt when I approached Lfivis that it was a most awkward thing that there should be no bridge joining the south shore of the St. Lawrence with the north shore, because that river interrupted the whole communication from the north. The construction of this bridge has been my dream, as well as the dream of every man in Quebec. As far as I am concerned I have no objection to the building of this bridge if it is honestly carried out and I would have no objection to the amount involved.
I would like the Minister of Finance to have a little conference with his late colleague the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals with regard to a pension scheme on the Intercolonial Railway. This Quebec bridge and the pension scheme on the Intercolonial should go hand in hand; they are both in the interest of transportation. The ex-Minister of Railways and Canals became very popular among the railway people in the maritime provinces ; they had great confidence in him, and I think it will be very hard for any other Minister of Railways and Canals to get so thoroughly into the confidence of the railway people as did the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, chiefly because he was broad enough and liberal enough to propose a system of pensions for the Intercolonial Railway men. I am told that when a man has served on the Intercolonial, especially on the new large engines, for twenty or twenty-five years, he is unfit to continue in that business or any other. And are we going to turn our public servants out upon the street, after serving this country for twenty years, without the slightest care ? In the interests of the transportation system of this country, we must look after the men who are engaged
upon the Intercolonial Railway. Although I am opposed to the government and to the Minister of Railways and Canals, as far as politics are concerned, I do not hesitate to support that measure and justify it as a wise expenditure of the public money of Canada. I have received a communication from a number of railway employees in Nova Scotia, asking me to obtain information as to how far that scheme has progressed. I understand that a scheme was prepared by the men, revised by the officers of the department, that a workable scheme had been developed by the officers of the department, and that it awaited the approval of the Minister of Railways and Canals and the subsequent approval of parliament. Of course, I understand that with the change that has taken place in the Department of Railways and Canals there may be a little delay, there must necessarily be a hiatus. I know hundreds of employees of the Intercolonial Railway who are anxious to take advantage of such a system as this but who inform me that they are unable to retire as they have no means of support and therefore it becomes very important that action should be taken in this matter because otherwise you will have a number of men employed on the Intercolonial who know that they are not fit to be entrusted with the duties they are discharging. But these men have no choice, they must continue at their posts, and therefore, I commend highly the far-seeing, statesmanlike view of the late Minister of Railways and Canals. Of course, I have had no personal communication with him, but I understand from association with the railway men, that he had approved of the general system of pensions for the Intercolonial Railway employees, of course without committing himself to the details. I approve of that scheme and I am prepared to justify it at any time and at any place. I would like to learn from the hon. minister and the ex-minister just what position this matter is now in.

I am aware that the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) had this subject under consideration, and had interviews with the railway officials about it. Passing from that matter to the subject immediately before us, I would like to say one word before I sit down. I am more than pleased to see that the proposal to ensure the construction of the bridge across the St. Lawrence river at Quebec, meets with such general favour on both sides of the House. I have been very warmly disposed towards the enterprise myself during all the time I was in the department, and my sympathy with it was owing to the fact that it meant a good deal for the advantage of the government railway system. I did not look beyond that at the moment, not do I think it necessary to look beyond it now, to justify the adoption of a sound scheme. I presume, from all I have heard to the contrary, that
there are no serious objections to this scheme to ensure the construction of the bridge. The extension of the government road to the Georgian bay, which hon. members know has been a pet idea of mine, is one which 1 think would be much strengthened by the construction of the bridge at Quebec. If we are to ensure over Canadian territory and by Canadian seaports the export of our western produce, it will always be necessary and important that this great water-way should be used. In using the water-ways of Canada, we must not lose sight of the port of Quebec as one of the most important to be found anywhere, standing as it does as compared with other important outlets through which this traffic will necessarily have to pass. The better and more adequately you equip that port, the more surely will you guarantee the future use of that port as a gateway for the imports and exports of Canada. As my hon. friend the Minister of Justice suggested, the port of Quebec is only accessible by one railway, but when this bridge is completed, with the splendid equipment with which it will be provided, in conjunction with the railway along the northern shores of the St. Lawrence, the port of Quebec will be second to none, in my opinion, upon this continent. When you provide an adequate and efficient equipment for a great port at the head of deep water navigation of the St. Lawrence, you guarantee that the people who have grain and other produce to ship will be able to do so speedily, and will be afforded economical means of getting their freight across the ocean.
Now there are one or two things which have been said in relation to this matter that I would like to allude to before pitting down. (Mr. Fowler) said that under this arrangement opportunities would be possible for a great deal of private benefit to be realized out of the profits which would accrue from the operation of the bridge. He instanced the case of what is called the St. John Railway and Bridge Company. be in this contract a clause similar to that which was originally put into the agreement under which that loan was made to this railway and bridge company, namely, that it should be optional with the government at any time, I think also subject to the approval of parliament, to take over that bridge upon paying to the company, or the individual members of the company, the amount of the loan which had been made, with an additional percentage to cover any reasonable claim as probable benefits that would have accrued to those who entered into the contract and carried it out. Well, it so happened that after the lapse of some years, and while that option was a living option, which might be exercised at any time in the future, it was deemed advisable for some reason or other, which reason I cannot state, because I never heard what the reason was, to expunge that clause from the contract, and the result is, that, notwithstanding, as the hon. member for King's has said, individual persons who made small subscriptions have been reaping handsome profits out of the undertaking, the government has no power to retake the property except under the general expropriation power which it possesses. I would hope that if a clause of this kind is inserted in the present agreement, empowering the government at any time in the future, particularly if the property be a paying one, to take it over, it will be accepted.

In this Bill the changes made, as compared with the resolution, consist in the inserting of the word ' bridges ' in a number of cases. For instance, in section 5, where it is provided that the subsidies may be granted to such companies as established to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council their abilities to construct and complete the said railways respectively, the word 'bridges' is added. In like manner the word ' bridge ' is inserted wherever the word ' railway ' occurs in a similar connection. Sly lion, friend, the leader of the opposition, asked very properly whether, in view of the provisions of the new Railway Act, we should adhere to the old drafting in the Subsidy Act. For example, where it requires that the rates be fixed by the Governor in Council, should we not replace the Governor in Council by ' the Railway Commission ' ? On reflection, we have concluded that it would be better to let the clause stand as it is, because we have a contractual obligation with the companies, by which their rates are subject to the supervision of the Governor in Council. There can be no harm possible, and good might come from leaving that clause as it is.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: The point I suggested was that you are retainnig the control of the Governor in Council while at the same time you have appointed a new tribunal to deal with the rates.
It creates a double supervision of rates, which may not be necessary, but which can do no harm.
You are giving the Governor in Council co-ordinate power with the Railway Commissioners.

I think it will mean that they will both exercise the same power. If it were not a matter of contract, the general provision of the Railway Act would apply, that all railway rates must be fixed by the board. But in this instance, there is a special contract, and we think that the obligation is one which should be retained. I do not think it creates any new power. The most that can be said is that it may be perhaps not necessary.

My recollection is that the resolutions bind the companies Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
to fix their rates in accordance with the order of the Governor in Council. The Governor in Council fixes the rates through the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. You retain that in the Subsidy Act, but at the same time you establish a different tribunal and take away the powers of the Governor in Council. You are creating a co ordinate jurisdiction, which may give rise to difficulties. I have not sufficiently considered the question to say that it will do so, but I remember curiously enough hearing exactly the same question debated in the Imperial House of Commons, some years ago, with regard to the government of Ireland Bill. They were establishing two jurisdictions, and the point raised was as to which jurisdiction was to prevail. Suppose the Railway Commission -would fix one set of rates and the Governor iu Council another, which is to prevail ?

The Bill providing for the establishment of a Railway Board has not yet got through the shoals of the Senate, and if any accident should happen there, we might fall back on the provisions of the Subsidy Act.

' We dealt with that contingency in the National Transcontinental Bill by providing that the Governor in Council, or such other authority as for the time being has power to regulate railway rates, shall have jurisdiction.
There is a provision in the Railway Bill providing for the establishment of a Railway Commission to take the position of the Governor in Council.

We might desire to have a more favourable rate than the average rate established by the board, and we might want to make it a matter of obligation that, in consideration of the subsidy, a railway company should charge a lower rate.
If the hon. gentleman desires to accomplish that result, he should use plainer language than he does in this statute. You may have disputes ns to which tribunal really should prevail.

Would this clause in the Railway Act have any bearing on the question, subsection 2, of section 8 :
,2. Whenever by an1 Act or document the Railway Committee of the Privy Council is given any power or authority, or any duty is cast upon it, in regard to any company, railway, matter or thing, the power or authority so given, or the duty so cast upon the said committee, may or shall, as the case may be, he exercised by the board.
The Minister of Justice is of opinion that that would apply in this case.

, The MINISTER OF JUSTICE. I think so. I do not think there can be any doubt about that. Both Acts will come into operation practically at the same time.

I have seen, but I cannot recollect the instance, declaration made in a statute that its general provisions shall apply to Acts passed during the same session. I do not know whether it is necessary, but I remember instances of that kind.

Except as to the amendments to which I have drawn attention, this Bill is an exact copy of the resolutions with whicli the House has already dealt, and unless lion, gentlemen wish the whole Bill read, we might safely adopt it.

I have no desire to have the whole Bill read, but the hon. minister will remember that when we adopted resolution 31, namely :
To the Tilsonburg, Lake Erie and Pacific Railway Company, for a line of railway from Woodstock northerly to a point on the Grand Trunk Railway at Berlin, or from Ingersoll to Stratford, or to any point on the Grand Trunk Railway between these places, not exceeding [DOT]35 miles, being in addition to, and continuation of the 9 miles mentioned in item 1 of this section.
-it was on the distinct understanding that the wording of this resolution might be changed. The contention was that this was a double-barrelled resolution, that it gave this railway company the power to hold up Woodstock, Berlin or Stratford, and get the one to bid against the other. I think that is a scarcely fair way in which to treat those municipalities. In my opinion the company should be restricted to a particular route and not be given alternative routes. I still hold to the idea that a subsidy having been granted from Ingersoll to Woodstock, the new subsidy provided in this case should extend from Woodstock north to Berlin, instead of going back to Ingersoll and running a road from there to Stratford. I assume if this clause be adopted, that possibly the road may never be built from Ingersoll to Woodstock. I do not know what the intentions of the promoters may be. but it would be absurd to run nine miles out to Woodstock and stop there. We have granted a subsidy already from Ingersoll to Woodstock, and this clause should be so amended as to provide for the road going on from Woodstock to Berlin.

1 am not in a position to recommend any change. The message I received from the hon. member who is much interested in this railway Act said that the wording, as it now stands in the Bill, had been submitted, after very careful consideration, on behalf
of the company. My hon. friend from Grey moved in amendment that this subsidy should be given for 35 miles northward to the Grand Trunk Railway by the most direct route. The hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Seagram) showed me a message which he had from the board of trade, urging that the company should be compelled to go by Berlin. On the other hand, I have a message from the Board of Tradle at Stratford urging the contrary. Under the circumstances, not having knowledge as to which is the best route in the public interest and in the interest of the company, I am not prepared to take the responsibility of deciding which should be adopted. I therefore hardly think that I can consider the rival interests of those1 who desire that this railway should go through their municipality, and I think we would be perfectly safe in standing by what we agreed to the other night. My hon. friend from Grey has had representations made to him as 1 have had to me, and on the whole we thought that we had better leave the resolution as it stands. I do not know who is going to choose between the-rival municipalities. I do not like to assume, not having any information that I could submit as an argument, that it would be better in the public interest the company should go one way or the other. I imagine that each municipality will look at rather its own interest, and it is rather late now to propose a change.

I think that to meet the wishes of the company I could move an amendment which would be more acceptable to them than the present proposition, namely that the subsidy be granted from the town of Collingwood for the distance provided in the Subsidy Bill, and that it apply from Collingwood for the distance mentioned here. That -would give them an opportunity of getting material more cheaply from Collingwood than they can now by extending the line to Ingersoll. I am satisfied the company would prefer that.

There is no one here representing the company ; and the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) having stated that this was submitted after careful consideration by the board and he himself being away ; I cannot support any change at present.

I have never considered the question of applying this subsidy from Collingwood southward. Even from Berlin to Collingwood, it would be a distance of upwards of 100 miles. That is a portion of the road for which this company has asked no subsidy.

The company pressed very hard for a subsidy from the present terminus to Collingwood. but there are a great many applications for subsidies. They have succeeded in building forty or fifty miles by means of

subsidies received from time to time, and I think it was felt that they might not get anything at all if they pressed for the whole this session.

I beg to move that the words in the third line of clause 31 ' From Ingersoll to Stratford or to any point on the Grand Trunk Railway between these places be struck out.' The clause would then read :
To the Tilsonsburg, Lake Erie and Pacific Railway Company, (or a line of railway from Woodstock northerly to a point on the Grand Trunk Railway at Berlin, not exceeding thirty-five miles, being in addition to and continuation of the nine miles mentioned in item 1 of this section.

Seventy-five to a hundred miles apart..

How far from Wiarton to Coliingwood ? It must be over 100 miles.

circumstances, and ask my kon. friends to vote for the resolution as submitted. I have not sufficient information to say which route should be adopted.
