Bill (No. 269) respecting the management and control of public and other works- (the Minister of Justice)-read the second time, and House went into Committee thereon.
On section I,

I wish to call attention to what I regard as a very material alteration in the responsibility for public works as affected by this Bill. This Bill purports to authorize the government, by Order in Council, to transfer matters within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works, for instance, to any other department. Parliament has seen lit to prescribe certain regulations with regard to all works within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works and these are established for the protection of the public. For example, in section 13 of the Act respecting public .works, the minister is compelled :
To invite tenders by public advertisement, for the execution of all works, except in cases of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest, or in which, from the nature of the work, it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and staff of the department.
There are various other clauses in the Act passed in the year 49 Victoria, chapter 36, for the protection of the public in the administration of the public works of the Dominion. Now, what do we find here ? The
Governor General in Council, if this Bill becomes law,
May at any time transfer the management, charge and direction of any public work, or any power, duty, or function with respect to any work or class of works, whether public or private,, which is assigned to, or vested by statute in, any minister or department, to any other minister or department ; and from the date appointed for that purpose by the Governor in Council, such power, duty, or function shall be transferred to, and vested in, such other minister or department.
Nearly all of the departments of the government are free from the restriction of any statutory provision, but it has been found necessary, or at all events expedient, in the interests of the public, that as regards the public works and as regards another department to which I need not refer here, but particularly as regards the Public Works Department, that there should be certain restrictions and certain provisions for the guidance and direction of those who administer that department. There are other departments which have no restrictions whatever. The Postmaster General, for example, has a free hand in almost everything he undertakes. The Minister of Inland Revenue has a free hand. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has a fairly free hand. And yet, by this Bill, the works pertaining to the Minister of Public Works may be transferred to any one of the ministers who have a free hand. The government may transfer the handling, the conduct of works involving millions of expenditure, without the provisions, without the restrictions, that would pertain to those works if they were administered under the department to which they properly belong.
Now, I think that this is a most material matter for the consideration of the House. I do not know why it should be found necessary at the present moment to bring in such a Bill as this ; I do not know any particular reason at the present moment why it should be necessary for the government to transfer from one department works that ordinarily belong to another department. But if it is necessary, if for any reason it is found that the minister administering one department of the government is unfit, or unable, or incapacitated from performing the functions relating to his department, and it is necessary to transfer some of his functions to another minister, I do not see why, in doing that, it should he necessary to deprive the public of the protection which has been deliberately and thoughtfully provided by parliament with respect to such works. I do not think that anybody will dispute that under this Bill, as it has been introduced, a minister to whom certain public works may be transferred, will bo absolutely free from the l'estrictions which would affect that work if performed in the department to which it properly belongs. The Minister of Pub-

lie Works may have authority to build canals and improve harbours, to do all works of that nature; but in letting out the contracts respecting those works he is bound by the restrictions and provisions of the Public Works Act. Apparently the government think that it will be convenient to transfer- those works to some other department. But there is not a word in this Bill, now introduced, that would provide for the public the protection in the other department that has been provided as regards the administration by the Minister of Public Works. Without any personal allusion whatever, I. may ask, why should the Minister of Public Works, who is bound by certain statutory provisions and restrictions, be enabled to transfer, for example, to the Minister of .Tustice the construction of enormous canal works, and that the Minister of Justice should thereby be enabled to let out those contracts, to accept tenders, to deal with the whole subject involving millions of dollars, perhaps without one restriction that would be applied to those works if they were carried out according to the statute I have referred to.
I do think, Mr. Chairman, that this Bill has been introduced without reflection, that it has been introduced for a particular purpose, to enable the government to transfer certain works from one department to another without the slightest sequence to the public. There is nothing in this Bill to indicate to what particular minister it is intended to transfer works or duties of the Minister of Public Works:	We may have suspicions upon
that point-I prefer not to deal with the suspicions-I do not care to what minister it is intended that the superintendence, or management, or whatever you may call it, of the Public Works Department shall be transferred, whether to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, to the Minister of Inland Revenue, to the Minister of Justice, or any other one. I say that under this Bill, when these ministers get the management of the works, they will be absolutely free from every provision that has been made in the statutes of this Dominion for the protection of the public. Now, I would like to ask the First Minister whether he really intends that. Surely when the Public Works Act was passed putting in certain restrictions and provisions for the protection of the public, to provide against, I may say, fraud-I do not hesitate to say fraud-to provide against an unreasonable letting of contracts or anything of that kind, it was the intention of parliament-to protect the public. There was -no question then, there was no intention then, to discriminate between one minister and another; the intention was that whoever should have the control of the expenditure of the enormous amount of money that is under the control of the Public Works Department, that whoever should have the power to expend that Mr. BARKER.
money, to distribute it to friends or opponents, should come within the provisions and restrictions of this Act. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that these few innocent looking words, the short provision of this Act. is intended, or at least calculated, to operate in removing every protection the public has, and I protest earnestly against the passage of a Bill of this kind in its present form.

My hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker), I think, is somewhat in error when he assumes that this is a departure from the established principles such as we find them in the Acts affecting the different departments. Let me refer him to chapter 24 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, the Act respecting the Department of Agriculture, where he will find that section 5 .provides absolutely for what may be done under the Bill introduced to-night:
The Governor in Council may at any time, assign any other duty or power to the Minister of Agriculture and may also assign any of the duties or powers hereinbefore enumerated to any other member of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada.
That is to say, by Order in Council it may be possible to take from the Minister of Agriculture some of the duties assigned to him by the Act repecting that department and hand them over to another minister. If my hon. friend will refer to the Act respecting the Secretary of State's Department, chapter 26 of the Revised Statutes, section 5, he will And a similar provision.	.

I do not dispute that the duties of the Minister of Agriculture might safely be transferred to other ministers, but the Department of Public Works and the Department of Agriculture are very different things. There is no comparison. The hon. Minister of Justice cannnot argue from the Department of Agriculture to the Department of Public Works. It may be reasonable to allow the Department of Agriculture to transfer the sowing of cabbage seeds or anything else to the Minister of Public Works or to the Minister of Justice.
I am afraid I would not be a success with the cabbages.
But to transfer the enormous works of the Department of Public Works to the Department of Agriculture is a different thing.

My hon. friend will observe that not only do we find that provision in the chapter which has reference to the Department of Agriculture but we find it also in the chapter which has reference to the Department of the Secretary of State.	.
Mr. BARKER, That is worse still.

I would like to draw his attention to the words of section 8 chapter 36 which is an Act respecting the Department of Public Works, because he will find something similar there. Section 8 of chapter 36 reads as follows :
If at any time a doubt arises whether the management, charge and direction of any public work belongs to the Minister of Public Works or to the Minister of Railways and Canals, the question shall be decided by the Governor in Council, and the works and property which shall be under the management, charge and direction of either minister may, from time to time, be determined in like manner.
Then the Act goes on to say :
And the Governor in Council may determine by which minister any power vested in the Minister of Public Works on the fifteenth day of May, one thousand eight hundred and seventy-nine, shall be exercised.
Provision being thus made for the transference by Order in Council of any of the functions or duties performed by one minister to the other. My hon. friend will And in the Act relating to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, chapter 25, the Revised Statutes, section 3, that the same provision exists. Not only is that the case but if my hon. friend will read section 3 of the Act respecting the Department of Marine and Fisheries he will find that if this Bill is intended to be applied to the Department of) Marine and Fisheries it is almost apparent that a transference can be made without new legislation at all by Order in Council. Section 3 reads as follows :
The duties, powers, and functions of the Department of Marine shall extend and apply to the subjects and boards and other public bodies, officers and other persons, and services of properties of the Crown, enumerated in the [DOT]schedule to this Act, of which the said department shall have the control, regulation, management and supervision.
What are the provisions of the schedule ? Sub-section 24 of the schedule provides :
That the minister may have assigned to him any other duty or power which the Governor in Council may assign to him.
So that, generally, the terms of the Act respecting the Department of Marine and Fisheries authorize what my hon. friend says ought not to be done. Then my hon. friend objected to this legislation on the ground that public interest would be safe' guarded by the provisions which are to be found in the Public Works Act in respect to tender. My hon. friend said that works which are now under the direction of the Department of Public Works ought to remain with the department because the provision of the law affording a safeguard in respect to tenders applicable to the Department of Public Works would not be applicable to any other department. If my hon. friend will turn again to the Act respecting the Department of Public Works,
chapter 36 of the Revised. Statules, section 13, he will find the following provision :
The minister shall invite tenders, by public advertisement, for the execution of all works, except in cases of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest, or in which, from the nature of the work, it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department.
That is the protection, as my hon. friend sees, that is contained in the Public Works Act. My hon. friend will see that the Act respecting the Department of Marine and Fisheries, section 5, is in terms similar to section 13 of the Public Works Act, so that the terrible calamity that my hon. friend imagines would result from a transference of a work belonging to the Department of Public Works to the Department of Marine and Fisheries would not take place because the same provision which exists in the Public Works Act in respect to tenders exists in the Act respecting the Department of Marine and Fisheries.

Does the hon. minister contend that every department of the government is subject to the same restrictions and provisions in regard to these various works that the Department of Public Works is subject to ? He may transfer under the operation of this Bill the operations of the Public Works Department to a department which is not subject) to these restrictions. That is what I object to.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think that the object of this Bill is the object indicated by the hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick). There is no doubt that in the definition given by the law of each of the departments of state, in so far as I recollect, at the end of each chapter defining the duties of each department it is stated that generally the Governor General can assign to the head of the department other duties.
Not in all cases.
I think it is in nearly every definition of the duties of the departments.
I do not think so.

I do not think there are many chapters defining the duties of the departments where that provision is not found. Nor is there any doubt that where doubt exists as to which department should be entrusted with certain works a special mode is provided in the law for defining the department which shall have charge of these works. That is not the object of this little Bill which appears to be a very innocent Bill, but it is intended to effect a very serious object. The object of this Bill is to take work which is clearly within the 1 functions of one department and by Order

in council transfer it to another department. It is very different from the case as pointed out by the hon. Minister of Justice, and it is very different from the case where there is doubt and tvhere the legislators provided a mode of solving that doubt. It is by Order in Council taking work which has been assigned to one department and transferring it to another. What is the reason ? This is the reason : When the present hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) came before the electors of the district of Maisonneuve it was charged against him that the department which he had undertaken was not as important a department as the one which was held by his predecessor and it was claimed before the electors of Maisonneuve that we had lost something and that some explanation should be given as to why a department less important than the other had been confided to that minister. He said at every public meeting that it was intended to transfer from the Department of Public Works to his department all the public works having reference to navigation-wharfs, bridges, in fact, according to the statement made by him to the electors, the Department of Public Works was virtually going to be transferred to his own department. He has not been able to cause that promise to materialize because the present hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) very properly has objected to breaking up his department. It is intended before the next general election to transfer all the works connected with navigation in and around Montreal to the Department of Marine and Fisheries by Order in Council and in face of the law which assigns these works to the Department of Public Works, in order to tell the electors that the government has broken up the Department of Public Works and has transferred all the works in and around Montreal and all the works connected with navigation from Montreal to Quebec, and as the hon. minister himself said, all the works connected with navigation from the Yukon to the Straits of Belle Isle, to his department. When the elections are over these works will, by Order in Council, be retransferred to the department of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works. That is the object of this Bill clearly and evidently and we claim, as my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has claimed, that the law ought to be contrary to that. It is for the parliament of Canada to assign to each department the duties which shall appertain to it. The ministry is but a Committee of this House; it belongs to the House alone to decide what attributes shall be given to each department of government. This is an attempt to obtain from the House power to switch over by Order in Council certain works from one department to another, for the purposes of the election, and afterwards to re-transfer them again. That Mr. MONK.
is why this Bill is introduced at the last moment.

If my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) looks into the statute constituting the different departments of government, lie will find several provisions to the effect that the attributes of one portfolio can be transferred to another, according to the judgment of the Governor in Council.
Then why do you want this V

That is the case in some instances but not in all. For instance, the mounted police are under the jurisdiction of the president of the council, but the very section which says that, enacts that the control of the mounted police can be transferred to any other minister as may be deemed advisable. There is therefore a good deal of latitude in that regard. It is not the object of this amendment to give to any minister the power to build and construct, which is now vested in the Minister of Public Works. The object is simply to enable another minister to manage and administer public works already in existence. I believe that to be a wise provision. If the departments were organized as I would wish, I would give to the Minister of Public Works the duty of building and constructing, but when the works have been constructed, I would transfer them to the different departments to which they belong. I would place wharfs under the control lof the Department of Mgirine and Fisheries; armouries under the Department of Militia and Defence, and post offices under the Postmaster General. But, I would not give to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries or to the Postmaster General the power of building and constructing. I would , reserve that exclusively for the Minister of' Public Works. If it were thought advisable that contracts should be given, then there would be no necessity for introducing this Bill. Every one will agree that it is far better to allow a minister to administer the works which come within the purview of his department. My hon. friend has said that und,er this law you could transfer to the Minister of Justice all the works of the Department of Agriculture. Parliament has already trusted the Governor in Council that no such absurdity would be committed, and I think parliament can trust the Governor in Council in this case. These general powers are often taken, but they are subject to the discretion of the Governor in Council, and subject always to the superior jurisdiction of this parliament. It seems to me, therefore, that there is no reason to say there is anything extraordinary in this legislation, and I think my hon. friend IMr. Barker) will, on reflection, agree with me.

If the First Minister had in view the transference of certain works

from one department to another concerned in similar works, this Bill would have been framed in very different words. This clause says :
The Governor in Council may at any time transfer the management, charge, and direction of any public work, or any power, duty, or function with respect to any work, or any class of works.
If the right hon. gentleman can -tell me any broader language that could be used for the transference of all the works of any class from the department of one minister to that of another, I would like him to tell me what those words are.	If the
hon. gentleman wishes power to transfer to the Department of Agriculture all the works concerning the harbours of Canada, he can use no better language. If the Governor in Council should see fit to transfer from the Railways and Canals Department the management of our canals, this Bill would authorize it. You can transfer any work from the Public Works Department to another department, and that without the restrictions which are provided in the statute for the guidance of the Department of Public Works. That is my point, and neither the Prime Minister nor the Minister of Justice has given an answer to it.

I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) that the words of this Bill are wide enough to transfer the entire jurisdiction with regard to any class of public works, from one department to another. The section provides that :
Any power, duty or function, with respect to any class of works, whether public or private.
. These words are ample to transfer all the wharfs under the control of the Department of Public Works to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and so on, I do not understand why this Bill should be necessary now. Is there likely to be any public emergency by which the delay between one session and another would be injurious to the public interest is such a matter ?
I submit that the proper course is to deal with each case by itself when the emergency arises, and to deal with it by legislation. If you desire, as my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier states is the intention of the government, to transfer part of the works now under the control of the Minister of Public Works to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, bring in your Bill for that purpose. If you desire to make any other transfers from one department to another, bring in your legislation for that purpose, and let the House deal with it. Why should the House delegate this power to the Governor in Council ? There seems to be no good reason for that, and no emergency is likely to occur which would make a delay from one session to the commencement of another session in any way injurious to the public interest. It does not seem to me that this statute is necessary. For the more
important departments there are provisions which have been found sufficient for the public interest up to the present time, and it seems to me that some explanation should be given as to the reason which induces the government at this time to bring in legislation of this character. What new feature is there in the transaction of public business which makes it desirable that legislation of this general character should be enacted ? No reason whatever has been given for it except that my hon. friend the Minister of Justice says that in respect of three or four departments legislation of an analogous character already exists. Well, has that legislation not been found sufficient ? What is the real reason for the introduction of this Bill, and what does the government propose to do under it ? If the government have nothing in mind which they propose to do under it, then the legislation should not be proceeded with. If they have any proposal before them with regard to the transfer of some works from one department to another, they should tell us the nature of their proposal. Unless they can assign some definite reason for such legislation, it seems to me to be unnecessary.

Let me say to my hon. friend that the reason for this legislation is to be found in the statute which has already been quoted, but which I will take the liberty of reading again in more detail, with regard to the Department of Agriculture. Section 4 of chapter 24 says :
The following subjects shall be under the control and direction of the Minister of Agriculture, that is to say :
1.	Agriculture.
2.	Immigration and emigration.
3.	Public health and quarantine.
1. The marine and immigrant hospital at Quebec.
5.	Arts and manufactories
6.	The census, statistics and the registration of statistics.
7.	Patents of invention.
8.	Copyright.
9.	Industrial designs and trade marks.
10.	Experimental farm stations.
This vests in the Department of Agriculture certain very extensive powers ; but the Act goes on to provide that it shall be iu the power of the Governor in Council to add to these duties of the Minister of Agriculture or to transfer to some other minister some of the duties assigned to him ; and this is the power proposed to be exercised under this legislation, if it becomes law. The subjects of immigration and emigration have been transferred by the Governor in Council from the Department of Agriculture to the Department of the Interior. Then, I think it would be more proper to have the Marine and Immigrant Hospital at Quebec transferred either to the Department of tlin Interior or to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. With regard to this Bill, my hon.

friend rroip Jacques Cartier says it is for the purpose of enlarging the Department of Marine and Fisheries. It will certainly be proper at some time or other to recast the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the Public Worts Department and the Department of Railways and Canals. At present a steamer leaving say Fort William for Quebec or below Quebec, while on the great lakes, is under the jurisdiction of the Marine and Fisheries Department; when it reaches the canals it is under the jurisdiction of the Department of Railways and Canals ; when it reaches the St. Lawrence between Montreal and Quebec, it is under the jurisdiction of the Public Works Department ; below Quebec it is under the jurisdiction of the Department of Marine and Fisheries again. I think this is very absurd. That steamer throughout its whole journey ought to be under the control of one department. It might have an accident at one place and another at another place, in which case it would have to deal with two departments instead of one. For my part, I think we should make these laws more in accordance with common sense, to say nothing else. In my opinion the Department of Public Works ought to be a great building department. But when a public building is put up, if it be a lighthouse, for instance, it ought to go to the Department of Marine and Fisheries for administration ; if a wharf, it ought to go to the same department ; if a drill shed, it ought to go to the Department of Militia ; if a post office, it ought to be put under the control of the Post Office Department. But to-day you have the absurdity of having the whole management of the post office building in the city of Toronto or in Charlottetown, or anywhere else, put under the Department of Public Works instead of the Post Office Department. All the caretakers and the menial officials are under the Department of Public Works. X would rather have the control of these buildings assigned to the respective departments to which they belong ; and this is the object of this legislation.

My right hon. friend refers to the statute relating to the Department of Agriculture. I hardly imagine the right hon. gentleman is serious in referring to that department as one to which we might transfer the public works of the country. Surely there is no analogy at all between the two departments. The provision in the Act relating to the Department of Agriculture, enabling the government to transfer to that department some other functions, means, I think, the transference of something analagous to the functions of the department. Surely he would not transfer to the Department of Agriculture the management of the railways of the country. No one would imagine that the Act respecting the Department of Agriculture would give the Governor in Council power to transfer to that department all the

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: railways of the country. If you can transfer the Public Works, you may transfer the Railways and any other department to the hon. gentleman who, with the assistance of the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell), manages the Department of Agriculture. The hon. gentleman refers to the Department of Railways as an analogous department. If the right hon. gentleman wishes to transfer from the Department of Public Works to the Railway Department, certain works, such as the harbours or anything of that kind, in some measure connected with railway work, let him bring in a Bill and it will receive rerespectful and careful consideration, and the right hon. gentleman may have some grounds for an argument in favour of the transference ; at all events, that question will receive careful consideration from the House. What I object to, and what I think ought to be objected to by every member in this House, is giving to the Governor in Council the power to transfer important duties and functions at will from one department to another. I do not wish to expend time upon the subject, it seems to me so clear that it would be an offence to hon. gentlemen opposite-I am sure It would be an offence to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House-to argue the thing. If there is anything whatever in the Public Works Department that can be properly transferred to any other department, let the right hon. gentleman bring down his Bill to again define the functions of the respective departments, and the House will pass upon it. Those functions are defined in the statues of the country ; they have not been left to the ministers to apportion. The right hon. gentleman wants to reverse all that parliament has, from time to time settled as to the functions of each department. The right hon. gentleman wants to take something, he does not tell us what, from one department and put it into another department. As parliament, when organizing these departments, said what the functions of each were to be, let us follow out that arrangement and when a change is needed let parliament make it, but the right hon. gentleman has no right to ask us to delegate that authority to the ministers of the day.

Might l ask the hon. gentleman if he has examined the Bill very closely, and if he has come to the conclusion that the words :
The Governor in Council may at any time transfer the management, charge and direction of any public work

would include the construction of a public work ?

But it goes on :
-or any power, duty or function with respect to any work or class of works.

Let me get down to that point. Would the words

I have just quoted include the building of a work? My own view is that they would not. They would mean to transfer the management and direction of a work after the work is completed.
It includes the wharfs in Montreal.
After their construction.

Suppose, as we find from the estimates is very often the case, one of these works is destroyed and we have to spend $40,000 or $50,000 in repairing it. [DOT] Would not the words even so far as we have gone include that ?

It is a question whether it would or would not. I am not prepared to say whether it would or would not. What I mean to say is that it does not seem to me that'these words would imply authority to carry on work of original construction.
Would the construction of the eastern section of the transcontinental railway be a public work ?

The eastern section of the transcontinental railway would be a public work ; construction is another question. The question I put now is whether the management and control of a public work includes construction ? It seems to me it does not. Then if you go on, you will see :
Or any power, duty or function with respect to any work or class of work whether public or private.
It seems to me that any power, duty or function would imply that sort of power, duty or function which the public works exercise, for instance, over public commissions like the Harbour Commission, at Montreal or Quebec. This does not include construction, but simply a sort of supervision or control over^what is done by these particular corporations. 1 quite understand that if these words can be construed so as to mean original construction, it would be necessary to go further and to add a section which would protect these particular public works. If my hon. friend thinks there is any danger in that direction, and that the provisions I have already pointed out as existing in one of the Acts at all events, is not sufficient, you might add :
And the provisions of the Public Works Act shall so far as they are applicable apply to any work or property, the maintenance, control, or management of which is hereby transferred.
So as to protect the public in the way he has indicated.
Does a public work mean a work completed ?

I want my hon. friend to realize that what is being transferred is the management or direction
4f>2
of public works. What it is important for him to consider is the meaning of the words 1 management, charge and direction.' Do either of these words include original construction ?

Those are not the important words, because they are not carried down into the latter part of the clause, as the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley) has just pointed out to me :
The Governor in Council may at any time transfer the management, charge and direction of any public work, or any power, duty, or function with respect to any work or class of works, whether public or private, which is assigned to, or vested by statute in, any minister or department, to any other minister or department; and from the date appointed for that purpose by the Governor in Council, such power, duty, or function shall be transferred to, and vested in, such other minster or department.
Leaving out altogether the words on which the Minister of Justice is laying so much stress, the important words are those which are repeated the second time in the section, and these it seems to me obviously include what is suggested by the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) whether the Minister of Justice thinks so or not. I think the first expression might include it, they certainly would include repairs, but the words in the latter part of the section undoubtedly include construction. I do npt think the Minister of Justice would venture to say they do not. How could you get wider words than the expression any power, duty or function with respect to any work or class of works.' I would defy any mail in this House to get a broader form' of expression, including construction and everything else, than these words. Beyond doubt, in my opinion, they include construction as well as management.

With all due respect to the Minister of Justice, I do not think it is possible to entertain any doubt on this point, that the management, charge or direction of any public work means the execution of that work. If my hon. friend has any doubt about that, if it is bis intention to transfer a public work to another department, why not use the word 'maintenance'? But the Minister of Justice will not make that change, because the Prime Minister has let the cat out of the bag; be has stated in reply to my own observation that it would be advisable to transfer the works connected with navigation between Quebec and Montreal, for instance, where several departments are interested, to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. That was the argument used in the Maisonneuve election, that is what is contemplated. But the^Minister of Public Works will not consent to a legislative change such as was promised by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and as he won't consent, it is contemplated to do it by Order in Council in order to carry us over the period of the next election. Will



my right bon. friend the Prime Minister state here upon bis responsibility, that it is not intended within the next six months to transfer some of the powers of the Minister of Public Works to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries ? If my right hon. friend will make that declaration, while I still consider that the Bill is useless and improvident, he would give me great satisfaction. My right hon. friend will not make that statement, because he has let the cat of the bag, and reveals that is what this Bill is for ; and I think that on the question of principle, as well as because it is an election dodge, it ought to be opposed.
I can say that if it is transferred, it will not be retransferred; it will remain transferred.

I would like to know whether my hon. friend the Minister of Justice will say that these words do not include ' instruction ' ? And if they do include instruction, why do you put to one side the safeguards which now surround the public works of the country?

I certainly think that the safeguards which are now provided in the Public Works Act ought to be put in here, and for that purpose I move that the following words be added to the first clause :
And the provisions of the Public Works Act shall so far as they are applicable apply to any work or property, the maintenance, repair, control or management of which shall be transferred under this Act.
Will the Minister of Justice tell us how much he is going to leave to the Minister of Public Works ?
That is not my business.
Amendment agreed to.
I think it is very important that these changes should he made only after very careful consideration, and I move in amendment that this law shall come into force on the 1st day of September, 1904.
Time can't wait.

The Minister of Marine aud Fisheries can't wait.
Amendment negatived.
Bill, as amended, reported, read the third time, and passed.

The determination of the government in relation to the tariff was announced at an early stage of the session,
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext:
and in accordance with the established practice in Canada the changes then proposed took effect immediately. But it becomes necessary for us to give more formal effect to them, as usual at the close of the session, by having the resolutions adopted and included in a Bill. I therefore beg to invite the attention of the Committee to the resolution which is placed upon the Notice paper, and which will be found on page 194 of the Votes and Proceedings, bearing date the 16th of April. It will be found that this is a resolution, put in proper form, for enactment of the few changes that were then announced, and I now desire to move that the resolution therein set forth be agreed to, with one amendment to which I desire to invite the atttention of the Committee. In the resolution providing for the imposition of a surtax upon certain foreign goods we rqad as follows :
Such surtax shall not apply to any goods actually purchased on or before the 16th day of April, 1903, by any corporation, firm or person in Canada for immediate transportation to Canada.
It was subsequently determined and so announced in the press that the thought contained in these words ' for immediate transportation to Canada ' should be expressed more definitely and therefore a circular was issued by my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) and announced in parliament at the time that in respect to these words ' for immediate transportation to Canada ' the privilege of importation without the surtax should be applied to all goods which were actually purchased prior to the date of the budget but which might not be imported into Canada until a later period, it being held that the orders' having been given and the contracts made a reasonable time should be allowed to permit importers to bring in their goods. We made no change in the principle that all goods not, actually purchased prior to that date should bear the surtax, but if they were actually purchased prior to the date that the duty was established the parties might have until the 30th of September to import their goods without the tax taking effect. That arrangement was carried out and I have reason to believe that it gave very general satisfaction to the trade which would otherwise have been very much embarrassed. I therefore propose to carry out the amendment by moving that the words 1 for immediate transportation to Canada ' be struck out and that the words ' if imported into Canada on or before September 30th, 1903,' be substituted. Otherwise the resolution stands as announced at the time of the budget.
What was the date announced ? My recollection was that it was the 15th September.
No, tile 30th.
Wliat was the position then-that the surtax would not apply to goods purchased at any time before tlie 30th September of this year ?

Not purchased before but imported before. To obtain exemption from the surtax purchase must have been made before the date of the budget, but the actual importation was permitted until the 30th .September. The date has since passed and the exemption is now practically at an end. The surtax applies to all goods that are imported.
I would like to ask the bon. minister whether any Order in Council was passed and what date it bears ?

An Order in Council was not formally passed for the reason that we could not pass an Order in Council until this Act passed. But following the practice of Canada in these things immediate action was taken upon the announcement in the budget. The regulations which were made had the same effect but they were not based upon an Order in Council, because, until the passing of this Act, we had no legal power to make an Order in Council.
Mi-. BORDEN (Halifax). Of course there is rather an anomaly in all these matters inasmuch as you have to pass an Act to indemnify yourself for an Act of illegality, and in this case there was a double illegality, because, in the first place, there is no statute and in the second place there is no Order in Council under the terms of a statute.
I see a good deal of controversy in the papers as to who pays this surtax and I would like the hon. minister's opinion on that point.
Just at the present moment it would be very convenient to accept my hon. friend's contention that the consumer does not pay the duty.

The hon. gentleman^ (Hon. Mr. Fielding) has really no convictions on the subject.
Resolution, as amended, agreed to.
On section 4,
What is the meaning of that ?

Under the Act of last session a license fee was substituted, but that Act did not at once come in force, it having been reserved for the imperial approval. We did not repeal the old section of the tariff, but the Act having since been approved, we will now collect the duty in the form of a license. There is one other resolution, notice of which has been given.
It has reference to the posters and handbills 462*
of an objectionable character. At present we can exclude such things when they are immoral, but it was represented to us by a deputation of gentlemen that it was not desirable to have the walls of our cities covered with pictures depicting crime. It was thought that easy familiarity with these scenes is not the best way of causing our youth to pursue the path of virtue, and we deemed it wise to provide for the exclusion of posters and handbills depicting scenes of crime or violence.
Is this intended as a covert attack upon the Conservative campaign literature.
No, although I am inclined to think that if one wanted to be critical, the literature referred to might be brought within the Criminal Code. However, we are in a generous frame of mind.
My hon. friend misunderstands me. The Conservative literature depicts scenes of crime and violence committed by the government.
It does not pass through the customs.
It may be comforting for my hon. friend (Mr. Borden) to know, that that home industry can still be carried on.

Yes, there is a very large factory on the other side of the House.

It's big enough to block a train.
Do you propose having it printed ?
The matter having been dealt with by legislation, I doubt that this very interesting report is so valuable now.
It might be interesting to have the experience of the one-eyed steer.

Mr. SPEAKER informed the House that the following message had been received from the Senate:
On resolution No. 20,

Before that is concurred in, I would like to bring to the attention of the government the fact that the employees of the Halifax post office forwarded to me some time ago a copy of a petition which they had presented to the Postmaster General, in which
They humbly and respectfully beg leave to reauest that the salaries paid to the employees of the outside service of the Post Office DeP^*' ment be increased to the same rate as those at present paid to the employees of -the inside service.
The petitioners mention two reasons on account of which they believe themselves to be justly entitled to the advance asked for, one the increased cost of living, the othei the responsibility of post office work, lney set forth in this petition that:
All classes of labour have been compelled to ask for -more wages to meet the increased cost of living; and in the case of post office officials whose duties require that they be at the office at a very early hour in the morning and a so late at night, it is necessary that they reside near the office, and to make this possible a higher house rent has to be paid. Those who cannot afford to pay this rent and have to occupy houses at a great distance from the office, or in the suburbs find it arduous to maintain a necessarily punctual attendance.
Tbey also set forth in the petition that the work is very irregular and strenuous, necessitating attendance at the office eat y in the morning and late at night the same dav, that the responsibilities and duties of the office are very great and severe and for these reasons tbey ask tlie consideration o tbe government. This subject, I think, was discussed to some extent in connection with the measure which was introduced by tb . Postmaster General with respect to the officers of the inside service. Tbe petition appears to give good ground for the consideration of tbe claims of these officers m the outside service; I know from my personal observation that their duties are in many cases very arduous, and I believe their salaries have not been increased, although the cost of living has greatly increased during the last eight or ten years. I therefore ask, on their behalf, the consideration of the government to the facts set forth in this petition.

I will call the attention of my hon. friend tlie Postmaster General to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax).
The Senate on the 22nd of October, 1996, resolved that a message be sent to the House of Commons to acquaint that House that another conference is desired with the House of Commons for the purpose of communicating to them the further reasons which induced the Senate to insist oil their amendments to the Bill entitled:
An Act to amen-d and consolidate the law respecting Railways,' and that the managers on the part of the Senate will -meet in room No. 8 of the Senate at eleven o'clock to-night.
The PRIME MINISTER moved that the House agree to the conference asked for by the Senate. [DOT]

I would like to ask, having regard to the peculiar formalities of these proceedings, whether it might not be necessary to take authority for what is called a free conference. It would appear from tlie ordinary procedure that one House simply submits resolutions adopted by that House to tbe other, and there appears to be sohie difficulty about any conference or discussion which might lead to some medium course. I would suggest to the right lion, gentleman who leads the House that it might be wise to give the managers of tlie conference some power for what is called a free discussion or free conference.

The suggestion is a good one, but for my part I confess that I am rather ignorant of these formalities. I have had no time lo look into tlie books to see what is to be done. But if we have power at this stage to move for a free conference, I would certainly add that to my motion.

The procedure, according to Bourinot, appears to be this ; That when a Bill is sent from the House of Coin-mons to tlie Senate and the Senate makes amendments to the Bill, in which they persist, then the House of Commons asks for a conference, and managers are appointed to go to the Senate to confer with the Senate and give reasons why they cannot consent to their amendments. If the first conference is unsuccessful, then the Senate lias a right to ask for a new conference, and to give the reasons why they persist in their amendments. That is what they are doing now, they are now asking for another conference with the House of Commons in order to give the reasons why they persist in tlieir amendment. After that, if there is no agreement, then a free conference can be held. Here is what Bourinot says :
The -report of the managers is then to he considered and disposed of by the House to which it is sent, which may take place immediately or be postponed to a future time. The result will

be communicated to the other House by a message. Sometimes a second conference will be necessary, when the first has not led to an arrangement between the Houses. Or a free conference may be held when two conferences have been fruitless.
After two conferences have been held a free conference may take place.

That Hon. Sir William Muloek, Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick, Hon. Mr. Fielding, Hon. Mr. Haggart, Hon. Mr. Blair, Mr. Borden (Halifax), Mr. Monk, Mr. Baker. Mr. Emmerson, Mr. Clark. Mr. Demers (St. John and Iberville), and Mr. Wade be managers of the conference on the part of the House of Commons.

The time fixed for holding the second conference between the two Houses on the question of certain amendments to the Bill (No. 21) intituled an Act to amend and consolidate the law respecting railways,' having come, the Clerk of the House will read the names of the managers on the part of this House.
The Clerk read the names.

The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick) on behalf of the managers of the conference presented the reasons of the Senate for insisting oil their amendments made to Bill (No. 21) entitled an Act to amend and consolidate the law respecting railways, as follows :-
1st. Under section 3 of the Bill as passed by both Houses the Act is made to apply to all persons, companies and railways (other than government railways) within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada.
2nd. Under section 4 as passed by the Commons and adopted by the Senate as section 6, the Act is also made to-apply to all local railways which may be declared works for the general advantage of Canada.
3rd. The above two sections cover the whole field of the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada on the subject matter at issue.
4th. Section 7, as passed by the Senate, applies to all local railways the principle applied to street railways and tramways by the Commons under section 7 of the original Bill.
5th. Section 6 of the Bill, as passed by the Commons, is objectionable on the ground that It seeks to make once for all, as applying to all local railways happening to cross or connect with federal railways, the declaration which under section 92, subsection 10 of the British North America Act, 1867, should be made only as to individual eases as they arise.
6th. The same section is also objectionable on the ground that it brings under the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada works owned and operated by corporations which remain creatures of provincial legislatures.
7th. The same section is objectionable on the further ground that the declaration in question would take permanent effect, although the crossing might be only temporary..
The Senate doth also insist on its amendment numbered 11 for the reason already assigned, and also for the following reasons
First : That the decisions of the Board of Railway Commissioners will from their nature apply to a multitude of cases and involve important interests.
Second : Because instead of being inconsistent with the spirit and with other provisions of the Bill, it merely extends the right of appeal provided for in the latter paragraph of sub-clause 3 of clause 44 of the original Bill to cases where leave Is obtained, from two judges of the Supreme Court of Canada, which right of appeal was limited in such original Bill to cases where leave was obtained from the board.
That a message be sent to the Senate requesting a free conference on the proposed amendments to Bill (No. 21) entitled : An Act to amend and consolidate the law respecting Railways.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. Speaker, I am perhaps able to report what in substance occurred at the conference that was held in one of the rooms of the Senate. It was decided that amendments 5, 6, and 7 of the Bill, should be accepted, and that the amendment with respect to the right of appeal, section 11, should not be accepted. The Senate concurred therein, and that clause will remain as when it left this House.

The report of the conference will go on the Orders to-morrow,

and I presume a motion will be made in accordance therewith.

Lest there be any misapprehension, I may be permitted to say that the House of Commons managers agreed that amendments 5, 6, and 7, of the Senate should be accepted. There was a modification, however, agreed upon by the Senate, accepted by the managers on behalf of this House, that section 5 of the original Bill was to be restored with some slight verbal alterations. That will appear in the report which the Minister of Justice will submit to the House in writing.

It would
be more satisfactory if a formal report would be made to-morrow.
That would be better, because it is desirable that it should be made to the Senate in exactly the same form in which it is made to this House, so as to prevent any misunderstanding hereafter.

It was fully expected that prorogation would be reached this afternoon, but because of an intimation given to us in the course of the conference with the Senate, it is not likely that we can have prorogation to-morrow, and that being the case, we may assume that it will take place on Saturday at an hour to be agreed upon at our next sitting. There is no object to be gained therefore by sitting later.
Then my hon. friend expects prorogation some time on Saturday ?

Yes.
